news.title: Oil edges down as investors weigh uncertainty over U.S.-Iran strikes
news.text:
BEIJING: Oil prices edged lower on Thursday as investors weighed the uncertainty of renewed military strikes between the US and Iran that ​risk disrupting supplies from the Middle East.

Brent crude futures fell 43 cents, ‌or 0.45%, to $95.2 a barrel at 0029 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 24 cents, or 0.26%, at $90.77.

The latest attacks were the most substantial exchange of fire between the US ​and Iran since July, with the war now in its seventh month.

Brent and ​WTI swung between gains of as much as $2 a barrel and losses ⁠of $1 a barrel during the previous trading session.

The session highs for both benchmarks ​were the highest since July 24.

Oil prices retreated on tentative signs that the latest flare-up ​was easing, with no confirmed exchange of fire since around midday on Wednesday, Sydney time, IG analyst Tony Sycamore said in a note.

US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that the renewed US campaign against ​Iran would not continue for “too long” and that US forces had targeted Iran’s radar ​and missile systems.

“We took out all of the new equipment that they tried to build along the ‌Strait ⁠of Hormuz - some defensive, some offensive … It was a very heavy attack last night, and we’re prepared to do another one any time we want,” Trump said.

“If that easing holds, and it is a big if, it won’t be long before oil moving out ​of the Strait via ​dark-ship transits and ⁠ship-to-ship transfers returns to the levels we saw at the end of last week,” Sycamore said.

Four commodity vessels transited the Strait of ​Hormuz, below the 10-day average of around 13, preliminary shipping data ​from Kpler ⁠showed on Wednesday.

Iran also added more ships to the list of vessels it deems non-compliant and subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they try to sail through the strait.

The US said ⁠on Tuesday ​that 17 million barrels of oil transited the ​Strait of Hormuz on Monday, calling it the largest volume of crude to pass through the waterway since the ​U.S.-Israeli war on Iran began.

news.title: IDF troops kill two Palestinian youths during settler raid, medics say
news.text:
Senator Chris Van Hollen on Wednesday condemned Israeli defense minister Israel Katz for reiterating his call for Palestinians to emigrate from Gaza as a "solution" earlier that day.

Van Hollen referred in a post on X to a report titled "The Netanyahu Government is Implementing a Plan to Ethnically Cleanse Gaza of Palestinians," which he released last year with Senator Jeff Merkley after visiting Gaza's border with Egypt.

"Now the Israeli Minister of Defense confirmed that's the goal. We must end our complicity," Van Hollen wrote.

In the report the senators published last year, they categorize Israel's policy in Gaza as ethnic cleansing.

The report criticized past statements by Israeli officials about Palestinians leaving Gaza voluntarily. "Any talk of 'voluntary departures' is a cruel hoax," the report read. "Departure is not 'voluntary' when the conditions needed to support life are extinguished."

Speaking Wednesday at a conference hosted by Israeli news site Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, Katz said that Israel is "fully organized and prepared" to move Palestinians out of Gaza "if it becomes possible."

Katz added the "accepting countries want U.S. support. Every country that is willing to accept Gazans wants American backing," adding that U.S. President Donald Trump "didn't cancel the plan at the moment; he has frozen it," amid pressure from "all the Arab countries."

Katz, who said that Egypt had pressured the Trump administration to oppose the emigration plan, also said that "it is being discussed all the time, including now, and I think that in the end, there is no other solution that will serve everyone's interests."

"80 percent of Gazans would like to emigrate, and we're checking that all the time in the polls. For this to happen, we need the United States – and the moment will come when it becomes clear that Hamas is not honoring its commitments. Then we will get the green light to move forward militarily, territorially and in other areas as well," Katz added.

Trump, who initially backed the permanent displacement of Palestinians from Gaza before the 20-point plan was announced in October, had since drawn back from the idea.

The new head of Israel's National Security Council, Shmuel Ben Ezra, convened defense establishment officials last month for an urgent meeting on the issue of "encouraging the voluntary emigration" of Palestinians from the Gaza Strip.

In a meeting attended by IDF and Shin Bet security service officials, Mossad officials said that no countries had been found that were willing to take in Gazans, and that there were no new developments around this issue. Officials were surprised at the short notice given by Ben Ezra, and that the issue was brought up again, since it had been discussed several times without any progress being made.

In March 2025, Israel's security cabinet approved the establishment of a "directorate for the voluntary emigration of Gaza residents." Its establishment was loudly proclaimed by Defense Minister Israel Katz with the purpose of preparing overland, maritime and aerial routes to third countries. But since its establishment no practical moves have been taken by the directorate, as far as is known. There were earlier reports of independent initiatives by right-wing organizations and nonprofit groups, but these involved insignificant numbers in comparison to Gaza's population.

news.title: How Trump's Approval Rating Has Changed With White Voters This Summer
news.text: President Donald Trump's approval rating among white voters has fallen 7 percentage points since the beginning of the summer, according to ActiVote polling, as other surveys have also pointed to weakening views of the president among a group central to his electoral coalition. In June, white respondents were nearly evenly divided on Trump's job performance, with 47 percent approving and 49 percent disapproving, according to ActiVote. By July, Trump's approval among the group had fallen 8 percentage points to 39 percent, while disapproval rose to 54 percent. ActiVote's August poll found 40 percent approved and 54 percent disapproved. The August poll was based on responses from 1,000 ActiVote users between August 1 and August 31. Participants rated Trump on a five-star scale, which ActiVote converted into standard approval and disapproval percentages. The July poll included 767 respondents, while the June poll included 478. The shift marks a change among a group that has consistently backed Trump. Fifty-five percent of white voters backed Trump in the 2024 presidential election, according to a Pew Research Center analysis of validated voters. Pew also found that white voters made up 71 percent of the 2024 electorate. Trump's weaker standing among white voters comes amid broader softness in his national approval ratings. The latest Economist/YouGov poll, conducted August 28-31, found 36 percent of Americans approved of Trump's job performance, while 60 percent disapproved. A Quinnipiac University poll conducted July 23-27 similarly found Trump's approval rating had fallen to the lowest level of his second term in the university's polling. The polling comes amid continued concerns about the economy and dissatisfaction with the war in Iran. The Quinnipiac survey found 60 percent of voters opposed U.S. military action in Iran, while 49 percent said they were financially worse off than a year earlier. What Other Polls Show An Economist/YouGov poll conducted July 25-27 found Trump's three-poll average net approval among white Americans had fallen to minus 14, which YouGov said was a new low. Among white Americans without college degrees, 43 percent approved of Trump's job performance while 52 percent disapproved. According to YouGov, Trump's three-poll average net approval among the group stood at -6, down from plus 27 during the first three weeks of his second term. Trump's standing among white Americans weakened further in August. An Economist/YouGov poll conducted August 7-10 found his net approval among white Americans had fallen to minus 19, which YouGov said was the lowest it had recorded for him among the group. What This Could Mean for Midterms White voters have been a remarkably consistent source of support for Trump across his three presidential campaigns. He won 54 percent of white voters in 2016 and 55 percent in both 2020 and 2024, according to Pew Research Center's analysis of validated voters. Even though Trump himself won't be on the ballot in November, could his recent polling numbers among that voting bloc affect Republican turnout or support for GOP candidates? D. Stephen Voss, a political science professor at the University of Kentucky, told Newsweek that the Republican base is rarely enough to secure victory in general elections, with candidates also needing support from less consistent Republican voters and, often, independents. “President Trump's low numbers naturally are going to be a problem for Republican candidates, as is always true for a president's party,” Voss said. “What’s unique this time around is that Trump's losing support among a different mix of voters than usual, seeing slippage in rural areas and among White voters without a college education,” he added. “The new pattern of presidential disapproval, if it proves durable, could hurt Republicans in districts where they've been strong for more than half a decade.” Trump Retains Strong Republican Support An Emerson College poll conducted August 16-17 found 86 percent of Republicans approved of Trump's job performance. Overall, 40 percent of likely voters approved and 56 percent disapproved. Economist/YouGov polling conducted August 14-17 similarly found 80 percent of Republicans approved of Trump. Support was even stronger among Republicans who identified as MAGA supporters, with 95 percent approving of Trump's job performance. Trump Pushes Back on Polls Trump has repeatedly criticized polls showing his approval rating declining. On August 30, he pushed back against recent polling in a Truth Social post. "THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA ARE OUT OF CONTROL, AND SOMETHING MUST BE DONE ABOUT IT. FCC TO THE RESCUE! President DJT," Trump wrote. A White House spokesperson pointed Newsweek to that post when contacted for comment on the recent polling numbers. Trump similarly criticized polling on August 24, accusing Democrats of "going CRAZY with Fake Polls." "They're putting them out at levels never seen before. They're called, 'Demoralization Operations,' where they try to demoralize Republicans so that they don't go out and vote — But the actual Polls are tremendous, and the Spirit in our Country has never been higher," Trump wrote. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Recent polling points to weakening support for the president among a key part of his electoral coalition.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: US judge partially halts Trump’s latest birthright citizenship order
news.text: A US federal judge on Wednesday (local time) blocked President Donald Trump’s latest attempt to restrict birthright citizenship, partially halting an executive order issued after the US Supreme Court rejected his broader effort to end the practice.US District Judge Deborah Boardman said the latest policy was “likely unconstitutional,” citing the Supreme Court’s August ruling against Trump’s earlier attempt to restrict birthright citizenship.However, Boardman allowed federal agencies to continue preparing guidance for implementing the policy. Her order applies to the certified class of legal challengers in the case, including children who would have been denied citizenship under Trump's original executive order.“If not enjoined as to the class, the 2026 Executive Order could deny the right to citizenship by birth to children whom the Supreme Court declared were citizens,” Boardman, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, wrote in her opinion.Through his latest executive action, Trump sought to tighten existing rules and narrow recognised exceptions to birthright citizenship, a principle under the 14th Amendment that grants citizenship to people born on US soil regardless of their parents' immigration status.Under the new order, federal agencies would not recognise the citizenship of children whose parents are not US citizens if either parent is “an alien enemy", “a foreign government employee", or involved in so-called birth tourism.Immediately after returning to White House in January last year, Trump issued an executive order seeking to deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents who were unlawfully present in the country or visiting under temporary status.The Supreme Court rejected that order by a 6-3 majority, holding it unconstitutional. Trump subsequently issued the narrower executive action that has been challenged in a federal court.A separate case challenging the new policy is also pending in New Hampshire.(With ANI inputs)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. news.title: US House Rejects Bid to Limit Supreme Court to Nine Justices
news.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - The US House of Representatives has rejected a Republican-backed effort to permanently set the number of Supreme Court justices at nine, amid a broader political debate over the court’s conservative majority.According to Al Jazeera, the proposal failed to secure the two-thirds majority required for a constitutional amendment, with lawmakers voting 212 in favor and 206 against. The vote largely followed party lines, with North Carolina Democrat Don Davis the only Democrat to support the measure.What Happened in the House Vote?Republicans introduced a joint resolution that would have amended the US Constitution to permanently limit the Supreme Court to nine justices.The proposal fell well short of the two-thirds support required for constitutional amendments. By contrast, ordinary legislation generally requires only a simple majority in the House.The vote came a day after the House approved a resolution condemning socialism by 220-192, with eight Democrats joining Republicans.House Speaker Mike Johnson criticized Democrats who opposed both measures, arguing that supporting the Constitution and defending the Supreme Court should not be controversial.Republicans' efforts have been viewed largely as political messaging ahead of the November midterm elections, seeking to put Democrats on record over issues including socialism and possible expansion of the Supreme Court.Why Is the Supreme Court’s Size Being Debated?The debate stems partly from calls by some Democrats to expand the Supreme Court in response to its conservative majority.The idea, often called “court packing” by opponents, gained renewed attention after former President Donald Trump appointed three justices during his first term. The conservative-leaning court subsequently delivered several legal victories to Trump.In 2021, four Democratic lawmakers introduced legislation that would have expanded the Supreme Court to 13 justices. They argued that the move would restore balance to the court after what they described as Republican efforts to reshape the judiciary.More recently, Democratic Senator Jim Clyburn of South Carolina backed the idea of a 13-member court, while former Vice President Kamala Harris said Democrats should have a serious discussion about expanding the court.Republicans have strongly opposed such proposals, arguing that changes could undermine the independence of the federal judiciary.Does the US Constitution Set the Number of Justices?No. Although the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court, it does not specify how many justices must sit on the court.Congress has therefore determined the court’s size through legislation over the country's history.The Judiciary Act of 1789 initially established a six-member Supreme Court, consisting of a chief justice and five associate justices. The number changed several times during the 19th century before Congress set the current number of nine justices in 1869.That history means the number of Supreme Court seats is not constitutionally fixed and can be changed by Congress without amending the Constitution.Has the Supreme Court Been Expanded Before?Yes. The size of the Supreme Court has changed several times since its creation.The most famous modern attempt to expand the court came from President Franklin D. Roosevelt after he won reelection in 1936.Roosevelt proposed adding justices based on the age of sitting members, potentially allowing up to six additional justices. The plan became known as the “court-packing” proposal and faced strong opposition.More recently, groups including the Brennan Center for Justice have advocated structural reforms such as term limits and ethics rules, while some Democratic lawmakers have continued to support expanding the court.The issue has now returned to the political spotlight as the United States approaches another closely watched midterm election.Read: US Supreme Court Allows Trump Ballroom Project to ProceedClick here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News
news.summary: US House rejects a Republican-backed bid to limit the Supreme Court to nine justices, amid a wider fight over the court's conservative majority.

news.title: Tiger Woods loses driver's license for five years in plea deal, avoids jail time
news.text:
Tiger Woods will have his license suspended for five years after reaching a plea deal in his impaired-driving case on Wednesday that will allow the decorated golfer to avoid jail time.

The 15-times major champion, who initially pleaded not guilty, entered a no-contest motion on all charges and was adjudicated guilty at a change-of-plea hearing he attended at Martin County Courthouse.

Judge Darren Steele said two five-year driver's license suspensions will run at the same time, one on a reckless driving charge and one on a careless driving citation.

"There are no exceptions. If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would go immediately back to jail," Steele told Woods.

The 50-year-old Woods, who was also handed about $1,500 in fines as part of the plea deal, has 30 days to appeal the ruling which dropped the more serious offense of driving under the influence.

WOODS ATTENDS HEARING WITH GIRLFRIEND VANESSA TRUMP

Woods, dressed in a dark suit and tie, arrived at the Martin County Courthouse seated in the front passenger seat of a black SUV and did not answer questions from reporters as he and girlfriend Vanessa Trump, the ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr., walked in and out of the building for the hearing.

State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl told reporters he was comfortable with the outcome of the case and outlined the prosecution's challenges in proving Woods, who has a documented pharmacological tolerance after multiple back and knee surgeries, was impaired by hydrocodone.

"Both toxicologists reviewing the information and evidence provided to them were of the opinion that there was insufficient proof," Bakkedahl said. “I don't make the facts; I accept them as they are brought to me of his impairment.”

Bakkedahl, who defended the handling of the case amid criticism that Woods could get favourable treatment given his fame, also had a message for the golfer.

"If I can send any message to Mr. Woods, it's simply this: of all the people in the world who should not get behind the wheel of the car, it's the gentleman who is one of the most recognizable faces on the planet," said Bakkedahl.

“Somebody will see him, whether it's in Georgia or Nevada or New York or where have you. He's not to drive a car.”

WOODS SPENT TIME OUTSIDE US TO SEEK TREATMENT

Woods, regarded as the greatest golfer of his generation and one of the most famous athletes on the planet, initially pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence charges stemming from his rollover crash in March.

At the time, Woods told authorities he was looking down at his phone and did not realise the truck in front of him had slowed down before his crash. No one was injured in the crash.

According to a probable cause affidavit, Woods had two hydrocodone pills in his pocket and officers observed him to be lethargic, slow, "sweating profusely" with eyes that were bloodshot, glassy and pupils that were "extremely dilated".

Steele had granted Woods' request to travel outside the United States to receive treatment in a controlled environment and, in a March statement, the golfer said he was stepping away to seek treatment and focus on his health.

In May, the judge granted prosecutors' request to subpoena Woods' prescription drug records, covering a period from the start of 2026 to March 27, the day Woods' Land Rover rolled over on a two-lane road near his Jupiter Island home in Florida.

In July, the judge granted a similar request that allowed prosecutors to obtain hospital records connected to the golfer's medical treatment following his crash.

Woods, who has not played in an official event since the 2024 British Open, has won 15 major championships, second only to Jack Nicklaus with 18. He also has won 82 PGA Tour events, a record he shares with Sam Snead.

He spent a record 683 weeks as world number one and is the only player to have held all four major titles at the same time, a feat known as the "Tiger Slam".

Source: Reuters
news.summary: Tiger Woods loses driver's license for five years in plea deal, avoids jail time

news.title: US Treasury issues $1 coin with Trump's face on it
news.text:
The US Treasury on Wednesday issued US$1 coins featuring the face of President Donald Trump, the latest move in an unprecedented campaign by the Republican billionaire to put his personal stamp on national institutions.

The coins were minted to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States, celebrated this year.

A roll of 25 US$1 coins was available for US$61 - a markup of 144 per cent - with a 100-coin bag available for US$154.50.

When the Treasury announced the plan, it was unclear if the coins would have monetary value or would be purely commemorative, but on Wednesday the US Mint said the coins were "also in circulation".

The move to put Trump's countenance on a coin with monetary value runs counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency.

Trump has aggressively defied precedent and legal challenges in his push to remake US institutions in his second term, putting his name on the Kennedy Center for the Arts and demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make room for a new ballroom, among other moves.

The new coin features Trump's face on one side, with the words "Liberty" and "In God We Trust." It also features the dates 1776-2026, marking 250 years of US independence.

The other side of the coin features a version of the US presidential seal, depicting an eagle clutching arrows and an olive branch, while covered by a shield that says "250".

This is just the latest in Trump's campaign to put his face and name on US currency.

In May, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said his department was pursuing a plan to issue a new US$250 bill with Trump's face on it.

He conceded that the move would require Congress to change the law barring living persons from appearing on currency.

The US Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether the new US$1 coin violates that law.

In March, the Treasury announced that US paper money would soon bear Trump's signature - another first for a sitting US president.

– with Agencies inputs
news.summary: US Treasury issues $1 coin with Trump's face on it

news.title: FAA seeks permanent airspace restrictions near Trump’s Mar-a-Lago as expert warns rules are ‘not good enough’
news.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has proposed permanent flight rules around President Donald J. Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida, to secure the airspace near Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate amid heightened concerns over unauthorized aircraft and rogue drones — moves that some say are insufficient to deter dedicated adversaries. The regulatory action was initiated at the request of the U.S. Secret Service, in the "interest of national security," the agency confirmed to Fox News Digital. "At the request of the U.S. Secret Service in the interest of national security, the FAA is proposing Special Air Traffic Rules for the airspace near Donald J. Trump International Airport (DJT)," an FAA spokesperson said. NORAD FIGHTER JETS INTERCEPT 2 AIRCRAFT NEAR TRUMP’S GOLF CLUB, 3RD PLANE DELAYS HIS NJ DEPARTURE Under the proposed mandate, a Special Flight Rules Area (SFRA) would be established. Aircraft flying below 2,000 feet within one nautical mile of the designated zone would be required to obtain explicit clearance, maintain two-way contact with air traffic control, and continuously transmit an assigned transponder code. Arriving and departing aircraft would also need to meet strict security criteria before entering the airspace. TRUMP HAS BECOME AMERICA'S MOST TARGETED LEADER, FACING THREATS EVERY FEW MONTHS The heightened precautions follow multiple threats against Trump, including a June plot where five suspects attempted to coordinate an ambush using explosive-laden drones aimed at targeting him and other high-profile officials during the UFC Freedom 250 event at the White House. However, drone experts argue that regulatory boundaries are "not good enough." AMERICA'S POWER GRID, FOOD SUPPLY AND MORE ARE UNDER THREAT FROM DRONES "When you look at what happened in Butler [Pennsylvania] it was discovered later on that the shooter had done very basic surveillance with a drone — a Chinese drone that you could buy off Amazon — before he conducted the attack against the president," Brett Velicovich, a former U.S. Army special operations intelligence analyst and drone expert, told Fox News Digital. Velicovich emphasized that government agencies must move faster to adopt active interdiction capabilities rather than relying solely on airspace designations. "We're going to have to have more counter-drone systems in place because it is not good enough simply for the FAA to send a message saying this area is a no-drone zone," he added. "When you're a bad actor, that doesn't matter." The FAA proposal remains open for public comment through Oct. 2. news.summary: The FAA proposed permanent flight rules near Donald J. Trump International Airport at Secret Service request, but drone expert warns it's may not be enough.

news.title: Straddling two horses
news.text:
The 26th Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) concluded in Bishkek on 1 September, marking 25 years of the grouping. The summit adopted the Bishkek Declaration — signed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi along with Chinese President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and six other members.

The declaration is stark. It expresses “deep concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran” and condemns “military strikes on the territory of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which has resulted in numerous civilian casualties and significant damage to the country’s economy.” It further states that such actions “violate the principles and norms of international law and the UN Charter and create serious risks to international peace, security and stability” — a clear reference to US-Israel operations. The SCO also backed a comprehensive and just settlement of Palestine, opposed unilateral coercive sanctions, and reaffirmed commitment to a multipolar world order.

For India, this signature sits uneasily. Just days before the Iran war escalated, Modi was in Israel, describing it as the ‘fatherland’ of India in a moment of hyperbolic bonhomie. How do these two statements — condemnation of strikes on Iran at Bishkek and celebration of Israel in Tel Aviv — sit together? That contradiction is at the heart of India’s current foreign policy dilemma. Understandably, heads of governments make hyperbolic statements in countries they visit. Diplomatic posturing, courtesies, the desire to please a host — all are part of statecraft.

But this is lot more than that. India-Israel ties have gone too deep to break. Defence, technology, agriculture, intelligence, diaspora — the relationship is strategic, not ceremonial. At the same time, India is part of a grouping whose members, except Pakistan which has mastered double standards, have no sympathy for US policies. The Bishkek Declaration is explicitly aimed at challenging America’s hegemony and unilateral action, endorsing Iran’s rights, and calling out sanctions.

India has been known for taking a moral, neutral and institutional position on global issues — non-alignment, Panchsheel, strategic autonomy with a conscience. That tradition appears to have been billed, for the time being. The other aspect of India’s foreign policy today is pursuing multi-alignment in a multipolar world. That may explain Modi’s desire to be in both camps — in Bishkek condemning strikes on Iran, and in Tel Aviv endorsing Israel’s right to self-defence; buying oil from Russia while buying arms from America; joining the Quad and also signing the Bishkek Declaration. I have two reactions to this.

One, a few strategic countries bordering big powers or in conflict with them have chosen their sides clearly. Take Sweden and Finland. For decades they practised ‘Finlandisation’ — forced neutrality to accommodate Soviet sensitivities. When that became untenable after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, they chose — they joined NATO to defend their territorial integrity. Neutrality has a shelf life when security is at stake. In SCO, all members except India are part of the camp opposed to the West. It is US President Donald Trump’s inexplicable strategy that propped up Pakistan as a peace-broker in the Iran war, further complicating India’s position.

Second, we should remember the dictum, “everybody’s friend is no one’s friend.” Multi-alignment cannot mean permanent ambiguity. At some point, credibility requires consistency. My contention is that a country like India, which seeks to take an ethical position in world affairs, should build and preserve its credibility. India’s image as a democracy, an inclusive and liberal society, a responsible power that speaks international law, should be nurtured. That moral capital took decades to build.

The overriding objective at Bishkek was to promote the concept of a multipolar world and mutual trade as against Trump’s unilateral policies. The deliberations focused on condemning attacks and sanctions on Iran and attacks on Palestine, but also on concrete steps — 28 documents were signed, including regulations for a new Universal Center for Countering Threats, an action plan for ports and logistics centers through 2030, a Green Technology Corridor, and crucially, statements on nuclear security and energy cooperation. With Iran as a full member and Russia and China present, the energy cooperation statement carries direct implications for US efforts to squeeze Iranian oil revenues.

The declaration also recalled the non-aligned nature of the organisation, while simultaneously pushing for an SCO Development Bank to facilitate local-currency trade settlements — a clear de-dollarisation push.

For India, which in June 2025 had refused to endorse an SCO statement condemning Israel for its attack on Iran, signing this time is a shift. In Bishkek, Modi also met Pezeshkian for the first time in two years, discussing regional stability and seafarers — a small signal that New Delhi wants to keep a channel open. New Delhi may be hoping that declarations in summits are diplomatic rituals — words that do not bind. One wished it were true. In today’s world, declarations are read in Washington, Tel Aviv and Brussels as alignment. India should choose right partners which will contribute to peace, growth and security of our country.

India cannot straddle two horses for long — one galloping towards Washington-Tel Aviv, the other towards Beijing-Moscow-Tehran. Multi-alignment must have a hierarchy. India’s core is with democracies, with international law, with freedom of navigation. Bishkek Declaration’s language on international law is fine; its geopolitical anti-West slant is not India’s natural home.

The Bishkek summit will be remembered for 25 years of SCO, but also for India’s awkward straddle. In a world where everybody wants India to choose, saying “we are everybody’s friend” may soon mean we are nobody’s reliable partner. Credibility, like trust, is hard to earn and easy to lose.

news.title: Woods loses driver’s licence for five years in plea deal, avoids jail time
news.text:
MARTIN COUNTY (Florida): Tiger Woods will have his license suspended for five years after reaching a plea deal in his impaired-driving case on Wednesday that will allow the decorated golfer to avoid jail time.

The 15-time major champion, who initially pleaded not guilty, entered a no-contest motion on all charges and was adjudicated guilty at a change-of-plea hearing he attended at Martin County Courthouse.

Judge Darren Steele said two five-year driver’s licence suspensions will run at the same time, one on a reckless driving charge and one on a careless driving citation.

“There are no exceptions. If you were to drive for any reason at all, you would go immediately back to jail,” Steele told Woods.

The 50-year-old Woods, who was also handed about $1,500 in fines as part of the plea deal, has 30 days to appeal the ruling which dropped the more serious offense of driving under the influence.

Woods, dressed in a dark suit and tie, arrived at the Martin County Courthouse seated in the front passenger seat of a black SUV and did not answer questions from reporters as he and girlfriend Vanessa Trump, the ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr, walked in and out of the building for the hearing.

State Attorney Thomas Bakkedahl told reporters he was comfortable with the outcome of the case and outlined the prosecution’s challenges in proving Woods, who has a documented pharmacological tolerance after multiple back and knee surgeries, was impaired by hydrocodone.

“Both toxicologists reviewing the information and evidence provided to them were of the opinion that there was insufficient proof,” Bakkedahl said. “I don’t make the facts; I accept them as they are brought to me of his impairment.”

Bakkedahl, who defended the handling of the case amid criticism that Woods could get favourable treatment given his fame, also had a message for the golfer.

“If I can send any message to Mr Woods, it’s simply this: of all the people in the world who should not get behind the wheel of the car, it’s the gentleman who is one of the most recognizable faces on the planet,” said Bakkedahl.

“Somebody will see him, whether it’s in Georgia or Nevada or New York or where have you. He’s not to drive a car.” 

Woods, regarded as the greatest golfer of his generation and one of the most famous athletes on the planet, initially pleaded not guilty to driving under the influence charges stemming from his rollover crash in March.

At the time, Woods told authorities he was looking down at his phone and did not realise the truck in front of him had slowed down before his crash. No one was injured in the crash.

According to a probable cause affidavit, Woods had two hydrocodone pills in his pocket and officers observed him to be lethargic, slow, “sweating profusely” with eyes that were bloodshot, glassy and pupils that were “extremely dilated”.

Steele had granted Woods’ request to travel outside the United States to receive treatment in a controlled environment and, in a March statement, the golfer said he was stepping away to seek treatment and focus on his health.

news.title: Iran terms US strike on wedding a ‘war crime’
news.text:
Centcom denies targeting civilians
• Iran to employ ‘new strategy’ after latest strikes
• US president floats renaming Hormuz ‘Trump Strait’

TEHRAN: Iran’s foreign ministry spokesman on Wednesday labelled a deadly US attack on a wedding ceremony in the south of the country a “war crime”.

The US attack in Sirik, southern Iran, killed four people and wounded 67.

“The truth of this unlawful war of choice — and the true face of the war crime — is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America’s desperate struggle to conceal its failure,” foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.

US Central Command (Centcom) denied targeting civilians, but Baqaei slammed the claim. Taking aim at Centcom spokesperson Tim Hawkins, he said the mouthpiece “has forgotten his own 

military record”, listing examples of drone strikes in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Meanwhile, Iran’s Red Crescent Society (IRCS), in a letter to the International Criminal Court, has called for legal action over the strike that it said constitute ‘a war crime’.

“Given the reported civilian character of the location as the venue of a family wedding ceremony, as well as the presence of civilians at the site, the incident raises serious concerns under international humanitarian law and warrants an independent, impartial, thorough, and effective investigation,” the IRCS said.

‘New strategy’

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei said the country would employ a ‘new strategy’ following the latest US strikes. 

“You will soon see that Iran’s new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade, will shatter your foundations,” Mr Rezaei wrote on X. 

Trump hints at uprising in Iran

US President Donald Trump later told reporters that the US “hit them hard last night, very hard. They gave a little love tap, but we hit them very hard last night.” The US launched the attack “because they took a shot at us in Jordan”, he added.

In response to a question, Trump suggested Iranian people may rise up against their leaders. “I understand their plight; they’re being shot… The regime is getting weaker and weaker by the day, and at some point they’re not going to be able to shoot so easily, because people aren’t going to take it,” he said.

On his Truth Social network, Trump suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as Trump Strait. “Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” he stated.

It is the latest geographical name change floated by Trump and comes a week after he ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” amid a trade war with Canada.

news.title: Tel Aviv signals its intent to occupy Gaza permanently
news.text:
Netanyahu vows to retain control during visit to besieged Palestinian enclave
• Defence minister says plans underway to remove Palestinians; urges US to find destination for the displaced

JERUSALEM: Israeli leaders on Wednesday signalled a permanent occupation of Gaza, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowing a lasting military grip and Defence Minister Israel Katz threatening the forced displacement of the territory’s Palestinian population.

Making his first visit to Gaza since the ceasefire began, Netanyahu made it clear a troop withdrawal is not on the table.

“We control the area. We are not retreating. We are staying on this line,” Netanyahu said near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates areas under Hamas and Israeli military control.

“We control 60pc of the strip, and we are not stopping, because we are eliminating the terrorists who threaten us, day in and day out.”

Despite the US-brokered ceasefire, Israel continues striking Gaza and making further inro-ads, insisting it must eliminate Hamas. Inter-national appeals to advance the US-led peace plan have not stopped Israel from targeting Palestinians.

Facing tight elections in October, Netanyahu rejected a proposal last month to advance the plan after Hamas agreed to hand over its weapons. The Israeli premier has vowed no military pullout until the group is genuinely disarmed.

“We are doing everything to reach our goal: disarming Hamas and demilitarising Gaza. Gaza will no longer pose a threat to Israel,” Netanyahu said Wednesday. “There is still work left to complete, and we will complete it.”

Ready to remove Palestinians

Meanwhile, Defence Minister Israel Katz said the country had plans to remove Palestinians from the Gaza Strip but was waiting for the United States to figure out where to take them.

“There is no real solution for Gaza in the end without this migration,” Katz told a conference hosted by the Israeli news site Ynet and the newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth.

The Israeli government “is organised and prepared to get them out by sea, by air, and by every way possible,” he said. The US Embassy referred requests for comment to the State Department in Washington.

At the start of his second term, US President Donald Trump stunned the world by calling for all 2 million Palestinians to leave Gaza, suggesting the Mediterranean territory be developed into a luxury resort.

He walked back the idea following pushback from Egypt, the only country besides Israel bordering Gaza.

Trump’s 20-point October ceasefire plan explicitly included no forced displacement. However, Katz claimed that Trump had only frozen the idea as he looks for host countries, adding that Egypt is not an option. “The plan hasn’t been cancelled; it is being discussed all the time, even now, and I think there is no other solution for everyone’s good,” Katz said. “But for it to happen, we need the US. When will we get their approval? Whenever it becomes clear that Hamas is not meeting its obligations.”

Katz claimed, without citing a source, that 80 per cent of people in Gaza wanted to leave but that Hamas was preventing them.

Similar suggestions that Gazans could be displaced have drawn international outrage. The proposal was condemned by Pale-stinians themselves, for whom any effort to force them off their land recalls the “Nakba”, or catastrophe — their mass displacement during Israel’s creation in 1948.

Forced displacement in occupied territory is a war crime under the Geneva Conventions. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and Katz’s predecessor, Yoav Gallant, over alleged war crimes, which Israel and the US deny.

On Tuesday, Israel said its forces captured the head of Hamas’s internal security apparatus during a Gaza City ground operation that Palestinian health officials said killed four people.

Hamas identified the man as Muein al-Ar--abid, an officer in the internal security service.

Israeli operations in Gaza have killed at least 1,334 people since the ceasefire took effect, according to the Palestinian territory’s health ministry. Ove-r--all, Israel’s offensive has claimed 73,470 lives in Gaza. The Israeli military has reported five deaths in its ranks.

news.title: The toxic cocktail that could blow up markets
news.text:
The starting point for any assessment of the levels of risk in the financial system is the amount of leverage within the system. It’s awash with debt and leverage.

Government debt in the post-pandemic era is at record and arguably unsustainable levels, with government debt alone nearly 100 per cent of global GDP. Total debt exceeds 300 per cent of global GDP.

While household balance sheets, globally, appear to be in reasonable shape, overall private sector debt, according to the International Monetary Fund, is above 140 per cent of global GDP, with non-financial corporate debt around 150 per cent of GDP.

The threat posed by overly leveraged governments and companies is a conventional one, albeit still threatening and with the level of that threat being exacerbated by the rising in bond yields and interest rates more generally flowing from Donald Trump’s trade war and real war-driven inflation.
news.summary: A letter from the Bank of England’s governor highlights the shaky ground that the global economy and financial system are on.

news.title: US government now 'trusts' Anthropic, the company that it banned months ago
news.text: In what can be called a major diplomatic reversal following months of bitter friction over artificial intelligence (AI) safety protocols and national defense boundaries, the Trump administration officially trusts Anthropic, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick confirmed this week. Speaking in an interview with Axios, Lutnick responded to a direct question whether he places confidence in Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei.“We trust Anthropic. They've done what we asked. They're back on the right side. So the answer is: Yes,” Lutnick responded. The remarks signal a major de-icing of ties that earlier this year resulted in sweeping export restrictions targeting Anthropic's most capable foundation models. As per the report, personal friction between top officials and corporate leaders had also compounded those clashes, driving the firm away from executive favour.Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown played key role in diplomatic turnaroundThe report says that the turnaround in relations arrived after Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown assumed a central role in managing the startup’s relationship with Washington. Lutnick showcased the improved alliance by personally introducing Brown before a global audience of dignitaries at the G20 Innovation Ministerial, inviting the co-founder to tell his story on the international stage, the report noted.In behind-the-scenes diplomacy, Brown proved critical in mending fences across official channels, reportedly conducting extensive bilateral discussions with Lutnick and National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.Taking the ministerial stage, Brown openly commended a Truth Social post shared by President Donald Trump praising data center expansion. Brown highlighted that advanced facilities generate tax revenues, create employment and are engineered to inject new electrical capacity into the grid.The shift comes amid shifting courtroom battles over prior regulatory crackdowns. A federal judge recently struck down the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic as a supply-chain hazard, determining that the punitive designation infringed upon the technology company’s constitutional protections.Anthropic is continuing to litigate an additional Pentagon designation invoked under a different statute before the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit.Get the latest technology news and updates. Additionally, a recent ruling from a federal judge invalidated the Pentagon's previous blacklisting of Anthropic, further solidifying its standing.

news.title: JD Vance Defends Donald Trump Depicting Himself as Jesus — Blames Prez's Unhinged Truth Social Rants on Aide
news.text:
JD Vance has defended Donald Trump depicting himself as Jesus in an AI image posted on Truth Social, RadarOnline.com can reveal.

The vice president, 80, was grilled about the Commander-in-Chief's erratic posts by a 22-year-old Liberty University graduate who runs a YouTube ministry.'The President Didn't Mean Any Offense'The veep was asked directly about the controversial picture by Bryce Crawford, who said the snap "made me upset" due to being a Christian.

Vance, 42, listened and then offered his perspective, saying: "I hear you, and I know the president didn't mean any offense." He pointed out Trump has consistently backed religious liberty and enjoys strong support from Christian voters.

The father-of-four then gave an insight into how Trump's social media accounts operate. The president fires off dozens of posts daily, often late into the night, but he does not personally vet every photo.'It Makes Me Upset As A Christian'Staff members curate content they believe will amuse Trump, according to reports.

Vance explained: "Sometimes he'll like chuckle at it, and sometimes if he really thinks it's funny, he'll have somebody post it. And that's exactly what happened here."

Vance shut down any notion that Trump deliberately compared himself to God. "Did Donald Trump mean to post a meme of himself as God? No," Vance stated. "He did not mean to, like, mock or mimic God. That's just not who he is."

Crawford remained skeptical of Trump's explanation that he mistook the image for a doctor depiction. "I don't know how he thought he was a doctor in the photo," Crawford said. "He was (wearing) a white robe with a red sash on it, you know, and that makes me upset as a Christian."Removing Post Showed Respect For Christian ConcernsThe evangelist eventually softened after hearing Vance's account. He acknowledged that Trump removing the post showed some level of respect for Christian concerns.

Previously, Vance defended another MAGA ally, Charlie Kirk's widow Erika.

Following her husband's death in September 2025, Erika was bombarded with questions about the circumstances leading up to Kirk's assassination. 

But Vance has now shut down the conspiracy theories.

Vance told former CIA analyst Buck Sexton on The Clay & Buck Show: "I'm most frustrated at the attacks on Erika and some of the other staff.“You know, Mikey (McCoy), who was Charlie’s chief of staff and a very good friend of both of ours. You know, Mikey was the person who called me and told me that he thought Charlie actually had a chance when he was in the hospital. You know, of course, that didn’t work out. But the idea that somehow these people were involved in Charlie’s death just enrages me."

Sexton pressed him about the ever-growing claims that something more insidious than just a standard assassination went down on the college campus where Kirk was killed. He claimed himself and his co-host, Clay Travis, were being driven mad by the swirling theories.

He cited a few, saying: "We take calls here, and people call in and say, ‘Oh, he had an exploding microphone on his body; it wasn’t actually a gun. It wasn’t really him that was doing the shooting; it was Israel.'"

Vance explained he felt the worst theories were the ones pointing toward Erika. "The idea that Erika has suffered not just the loss of Charlie, but all this B.S. that's directed at her, that's very frustrating to me," Vance said.
news.summary: JD Vance has defended Donald Trump depicting himself as Jesus in an AI image posted on Truth Social during an interview with a Christian YouTube show host.

news.title: Outdoor gear retailer Patagonia sues Trump for shrinking beloved Utah national monument managed by tribes
news.text:
Outdoor retailer Patagonia joined a coalition of Indigenous and environmental groups suing the Trump administration on Wednesday over its decision this summer to massively shrink two national monuments in Utah, Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante.

“What is happening in Utah is tragic,” Patagonia CEO Ryan Gellert wrote in a blog post on Wednesday of his company’s suit, which concerns the Bears Ears decision. “President Donald Trump’s proclamations all but eliminating Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monuments betray Tribal sovereignty and scrap years of work to create groundbreaking management plans for some of the most culturally significant places in the country.”

In July, the Trump administration shrunk each monument by about 90 percent, opening millions of acres of public lands to oil drilling, uranium mining and other developments. 

The suits seek to revive 2017 litigation challenging the first Trump administration’s attempts to shrink the monuments, arguing that President Trump lacks the legal authority to downsize the protected lands. The original suits were put on hold when the Biden administration reversed course from Trump and expanded the monuments. 

Patagonia argues that the Antiquities Act, which gave Presidents Barack Obama and Bill Clinton the power to create Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante, respectively, contains no power to undo a monument designation. 

The Independent has contacted the White House, Interior Department and Justice Department for comment.

A variety of Indigenous peoples consider the lands within both monuments sacred. 

Bears Ears was the first national monument created at the request of Native American nations, after the Hopi Tribe, Navajo Nation, Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, Ute Indian Tribe and the Pueblo of Zuni successfully petitioned the Obama administration. 

It was also the first national monument in U.S. history to be co-managed by Native American nations themselves, considered a watershed moment after centuries of the U.S. government dispossessing Indigenous peoples. 

“It’s been disappointing to see how much work has been put into trying to do co-management with the tribes and the federal agencies, and then having all that work put on hold or shelved,” Angelo Baca, an enrolled citizen of the Navajo Nation and member of the Hopi Tribe, told the Salt Lake Tribune on Wednesday. 

Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, as well as the state’s congressional delegation, supported the Trump administration’s move to shrink the monuments.

The Trump administration and its allies have argued that the Utah lands contain important resources and that past Democratic administrations exceeded the intended scope of the Antiquities Act.

“The Bears Ears region contains several resources that are vital to energy and resource independence and, in turn, critical to national security,” the president wrote in the order shrinking the monument. 

“It’s very clear that these monument designations are supposed to be the smallest area possible to protect the antiquities, and these multi-million-acre monuments that are bigger than the state of Delaware certainly do not fit that designation,” Gov. Cox said at a July signing ceremony for the changes. 

At least nine mining claims have been filed on lands that were protected until the Trump administration policy shift this summer.

Patagonia argues the Trump administration decision around the Utah lands is part of a larger attack on the environment that has seen the White House cancel renewables projects and attempt to pull back on regulating greenhouse gases.

“Since the first week of this administration, we have witnessed an aggressive whole-of-government campaign against protecting this nation’s critical air, water and land resources, including the undoing of environmental regulation, climate action and public land protection that will take years if not decades to undo,” Gellert wrote.
news.summary: Patagonia was among the groups that sued the first Trump administration to block a similar move

news.title: MARK RILEY: Why voters are turning to One Nation and what the major parties need to do to win them back
news.text:
As they sift through the wreckage of last weekend’s Secret Harbour by-election in WA, political strategists from both sides of the fence are asking themselves the same questions.

Who exactly are these legions of new One Nation voters and what has driven them to join Pauline Hanson’s rampaging orange army?

And, more importantly, what do they need to do to win them back?

A survey this week from pollster John Utting and former Labor adviser Bruce Hawker of 1014 One Nation voters has provided some fascinating answers.

The results confirm many of the general assumptions about why so many voters are peeling away from the major parties.

But they also deliver some hope for the Liberal, National and Labor parties that a considerable proportion could be lured back.

The traditional parties just have to listen to what these disaffected voters are saying and respond in ways that provide practical solutions that are in keeping with their political values.

In other words, don’t just try to become One Nation-lite. Be better, more effective versions of yourself.

The survey builds a profile of the average One Nation voter.

He is most likely male, aged in his late fifties, lives outside the major cities, is most often a tradie who didn’t go to university, owns or is paying off his own house, only speaks English at home and describes his cultural identity as: “Australian”.

Just 38 per cent of One Nation voters are women and the largest age cohort of both genders is over-65. Only 17 per cent are younger than 35.

Seventy per cent either voted for another party at the 2025 election or didn’t vote at all.

Thirty-eight per cent voted for the Liberals or Nationals and 17 per cent for Labor.

The one issue they nominate more than any other for driving their change in voting preference is immigration.

It is the subject that now defines the political battle among the parties to become the rightful custodians of Australian patriotism.

An almost three-quarter majority of respondents say they want migration numbers “substantially reduced” and foreigners banned from buying Australian homes.

The same majority wants the Welcome to Country banned.

“You’ve got people who want to tell us what sort of country this is going to be. Nobody asked us whether we wanted the country changed so much!” one respondent says.

“You walk through parts of the city and it doesn’t feel like the same place,” says another.

“If you object you’re a racist, so most people say nothing and vote quietly,” adds another.

But there are other parts of the One Nation platform that the new converts are much less comfortable with.

Its policies on abortion, domestic violence, the minimum wage and Donald Trump are big turn-offs.

Many disagreed with Pauline Hanson’s recent comments on limiting a woman’s right to choose, that domestic violence was “a two-way street” and her positions against minimum wage rises and in favour of greater powers for bosses to sack “lazy workers”.

All those issues fall within Labor’s traditional agenda. Expect Anthony Albanese and his ministers to run hard on them as the 2028 election nears.

More than half of all One Nation supporters don’t like Pauline Hanson’s close alliance with Donald Trump.

Expect to hear his name raised more frequently, too.

Former Coalition supporters say they would have another look at the Liberals and Nationals if they took strong stands on limiting migration and addressing the cost of living.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has promised to deliver deep cuts to migration when he eventually releases his policy.

But that presents another dilemma. The challenge for him is to change policy without changing the character of his party so much that it drives away the more progressive section of his base that has stuck with him during the stampede to One Nation.

And there is a softness in Pauline Hanson’s support.

Fifty-two per cent of respondents say they are “absolutely certain” of voting One Nation at the next election, which means 48 per cent aren’t.

That is where the opportunity lies for the Coalition and Labor.

There are opportunities and risks for all parties, but after the major party shellacking in Secret Harbour the enormity of the challenge is no secret to anyone.

Mark Riley is the Seven Network’s political editor
news.summary: MARK RILEY: The WA by-election shows One Nation is a force to be reckoned with. But they’re not unstoppable.

news.title: US export curbs have reshaped China’s tech scene around ‘chokepoints’: report
news.text:
Chinese technology companies seeking public listings are increasingly concentrated in areas where Beijing is trying to break its reliance on foreign technology, as years of US export controls reshape the country’s pipeline of stock market hopefuls.
About 20 per cent of companies that have launched initial public offerings on Shanghai’s Star Market so far this year are engaged in tackling key technological “chokepoints” facing China, compared with just 8.1 per cent in 2022, according to a Morgan Stanley analysis of 229 IPOs between 2022 and mid-July 2026.
About 60 per cent of firms in 2026 contributed to China’s push for supply chain self-sufficiency, up from 41 per cent four years ago, said the report published on Friday.
China’s critical tech bottlenecks have also narrowed since 2022, from a broad mix of strategic goods to a focus on the semiconductor supply chain, according to the report. Driven by expanding foreign trade curbs, the pressure points have moved upstream to raw materials, complex machinery, specialised parts and core manufacturing tools.
Of the 21 companies Morgan Stanley identified as addressing chokepoints this year, 19 are in the semiconductor supply chain. There is a particular focus on chokepoints in electronics, with 15 of the firms coming from that sector.
“As the chokepoints expanded in the past three to four years, more domestic companies became dedicated in those areas and by 2026 some of them had grown to a stage ready to tap into the capital market to further scale up,” Morgan Stanley analysts wrote.
Washington has imposed sweeping controls on China’s semiconductor sector since 2022, restricting the country’s access to advanced computing chips and the equipment needed to manufacture cutting-edge semiconductors.
A major escalation in December 2024 restricted various chipmaking equipment and categories of semiconductor-development software.
The administration of US President Joe Biden further curbed access to high-bandwidth memory used for artificial intelligence and blacklisted Chinese organisations including semiconductor factories, equipment manufacturers, and investment firms linked to China’s military ambitions.

While US President Donald Trump has since eased some restrictions on advanced AI processors, including allowing Nvidia’s H200 chips to be sold to China under certain conditions, the broader pressure on the supply chain remains.
Soaring R&D costs
The report also found that China’s technological push was becoming increasingly expensive – and risky.
Companies in the 2026 IPO cohort spent twice as much on research and development on average compared with their 2022 counterparts, while R&D spending per employee also doubled, according to Morgan Stanley.
Annual pre-IPO capital expenditure for companies in 2026 stood at 716 million yuan (US$107 million), more than four times the 174 million yuan average recorded for the 2022 cohort.
Morgan Stanley analysts said the heavier spending reflected a “genuine need” for capital, as companies working deeper in strategic supply chains required significant investment not only in research but also to scale their technologies into commercial production.
For example, the blockbuster IPO of chipmaker ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) in July showed how capital raised through public markets could help expand its dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) production capacity.
The expansion could benefit Chinese chipmaking-equipment suppliers seeking to replace US vendors across more stages of production, although there was still a lack of domestic alternatives in deep-ultraviolet lithography equipment, the analysts said.
However, the new generation of listings comes with greater risks for investors.
Only 46 per cent of the 2026 companies were profitable at scale, down from 72 per cent in 2022. Their median return on equity (ROE) – a key measure of net profit generated per dollar of shareholder investment – was 10 percentage points lower than the 2022 batch, with average ROE down by more than 17 percentage points.
The numbers suggest many firms are less commercially proven despite their technological progress, according to the report.
“We think eventually it is commercial validation that will drive post-IPO performance and investor interest in new IPOs,” the analysts said.

news.title: Iran, US trade threats as Tehran blames Washington for wedding strike
news.text:
Iran and the United States traded threats on Wednesday after some of the heaviest military exchanges in weeks, including a strike on a wedding party that Tehran blamed on Washington and branded a "war crime."

President Donald Trump said US forces staged a "very heavy attack" on Iranian targets overnight and are "prepared to do another one any time we want."

Iran's security chief warned that the United States would face a "new strategy" in the war that began in late February with US and Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic.

"You will soon see that Iran's new strategy on the battlefield, in diplomacy and in confronting the economic blockade will shatter your foundations," Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei wrote on X.

Besides threatening new attacks, Trump on Wednesday also suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz, the vital oil waterway that Tehran has effectively shut for six months, as "Trump Strait."

"Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???" the US president said in a post on Truth Social.

Read moreUS-Iran war: Old videos falsely claim to show new attacks on American bases

He later implied that he wasn't serious. "It was just thrown out there," Trump told an AFP reporter who asked about his post.

Iran targeted US bases in Jordan, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq's autonomous Kurdistan region after extensive US bombardment on Tuesday of sites across Iran.

Iran reacted with fury after the Iranian Red Crescent said four people including a child were killed and more than 50 people wounded by a US attack that hit a wedding in Iran's south. 

"The truth of this unlawful war of choice -- and the true face of the war crime -- is in Sirik, where a wedding ceremony was brutally bombed as part of America's desperate struggle to conceal its failure," foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei posted on X.

The US military did not address the incident directly. 

US Central Command (CENTCOM) spokesman Tim Hawkins said "the US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC," referring to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

'Acts like Satan' 

Iran's top negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf lashed out at Washington over the wedding attack, calling the United States "Satan." 

"If a power acts like Satan, picks targets like Satan, and kills like Satan, it's Satan," he posted on X. 

The latest round of fighting began when Washington hit Iranian targets on Sunday, the first known strikes in several weeks. 

Tehran's forces then targeted US troops in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates, and projectiles struck two oil tankers in unclaimed attacks, one of which killed two Filipino sailors, according to a Saudi shipping company.

Trump said the US strikes were in retaliation for an Iranian attempt to plant sea mines in the Strait and for firing missiles at a base in Jordan.

Read moreIsraeli FM Gideon Sa'ar: 'I hope Iran will not make the mistake of attacking us'

Iranians expressed regret at the return to hostilities.

Hossein Moazami, 50, who is self-employed, called the attacks "truly distressing."

"I hope they all return to the negotiating table because the only people suffering from this are the Iranian people," he said. "The Americans are on the other side of the world and nothing happens to them."

A video shared by an Iranian government account showed debris and damage at what it said was the wedding site in Sirik following the US strike, with people heard screaming in the background. 

"It is a very saddening incident...Thank God the casualties were not higher," Ali Mallahi, father of the bride and owner of the building that was hit, said in a video carried by state TV.

The war began February 28 with US-Israeli attacks on Iran that killed its supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. 

A fragile ceasefire collapsed after attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of world oil supplies previously flowed.

Israel's defence minister said meanwhile that his country was prepared to respond "with great force" if attacked by Iran over the Jewish high holiday season, which begins in mid-September.

"For now, they are striking throughout the region except us," Israel Katz told a conference hosted by Israeli media outlets.

(FRANCE 24 with AFP)
news.summary: Iran and the United States traded threats on Wednesday after their heaviest military exchanges in weeks. Tehran accused Washington of striking a wedding party and called the attack a war crime. President Donald Trump threatened further US strikes, while Iran’s security chief warned Washington would face a “new strategy.”

news.title: Trump vows to hit campaign trail hard for Republicans in tight midterms
news.text:
Donald Trump faced weak approval ratings, with just 33% of Americans approving of his performance in an August poll, the lowest of his political career. (EPA Images pic)
WASHINGTON: US president Donald Trump vowed on Wednesday to campaign aggressively for Republican candidates ahead of November's midterm elections, saying he has planned extensive travel to states with high-stakes races.
At a White House dinner for congressional Republicans, Trump touted his success campaigning for the party and promised a busy schedule of appearances in the final month, similar to his own non-stop 2024 campaign.
"I will be with you 100% all the way to November," Trump told the crowd, which included Republican lawmakers such as Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Tom Barrett who represent some of the most competitive districts.
"It's all about 35 races.... We are going to see if we can get everyone elected," Trump added, referring to congressional contests.
The president faces weak approval ratings over the Iran war and persistent inflation. That worries Republicans who are fighting to ​preserve their party's narrow congressional majorities in the November 3 votes.
Just 33% of Americans approved of Trump's performance in a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Aug 31, the lowest of his political career and the third straight month at that level.
Trump's Iran war has disrupted global oil supplies, raising US energy prices and deepening a US cost-of-living crisis. The conflict has entered its seventh month with no imminent diplomatic efforts to end it in sight. Washington and Tehran havein the past days exchanged their biggest barrage of fire since July, renewing concerns of full-fledged war.
Trump has in recent weeks travelled to Texas, where he headlined a fundraiser for state attorney general Ken Paxton, who is running for US Senate. The president also went to South Carolina to campaign for Darline Graham in a US Senate primary runoff, which she won. She seeks to win the Senate seat of her late brother, Lindsey Graham, in November.
"I'll be making a lot of stops," Trump told reporters earlier Wednesday in the Oval Office. Among those will be a campaign visit to Alaska on behalf of incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan. He added that he will also stump for "a few governors."
"I love the governors, but we're interested in the Senate, and we're interested in the House," Trump said.
The president is now set to speak on both nights of ‌the Republican Party's unusual midterm convention next week, a change that some insiders attributed to concerns over the Republican National Committee's ability to attract members and activists to the event.
news.summary: The US president plans extensive travel to states with high-stakes contests, similar to his own non-stop 2024 campaign.
