news.title: A judge blocks Trump's new bid to curb birthright citizenship, citing Supreme Court precedent
news.text:
A federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to limit birthright citizenship, granting a preliminary injunction against an executive order that the administration said would target “birth tourism.”

U.S. District Judge Deborah L. Boardman in Maryland on Wednesday issued the injunction until a class-action lawsuit brought by immigrant families and advocacy groups is resolved. 

“The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are ‘citizens at birth,’” Boardman, appointed by President Joe Biden, wrote in Wednesday's ruling. 

Birthright citizenship is guaranteed under current law for anyone who is born on U.S. soil, with a few exceptions. The law stretches back to 1868, when the 14th Amendment was ratified in the aftermath of the Civil War. 

But Trump has long wanted to end birthright citizenship, issuing a previous executive order declaring that children born to people who are in the United States illegally or temporarily are not American citizens. The Supreme Court struck down that attempt in June.

In August, the president tried again with a narrowed executive order that appeared to restrict automatic citizenship for specific categories of people, including children born to adults with connections to foreign embassies or organizations or to anyone considered an “alien enemy” of the United States. 

The order defined birth tourism as someone who enters the United States on a “nonimmigrant visa for the purpose of giving birth on American soil.” Birth tourism is already considered fraud and grounds to restrict a visa if someone seeks one specifically to obtain U.S. citizenship for a child. 

The order sought to deny citizenship to children born to adults who “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship,” and some families said they feared their children could be denied citizenship simply because they purchased airfare to come to the U.S. and got pregnant after they arrived. 

Families and organizations who sued over the birthright citizenship restrictions told the court that the executive branch has taken a broad view of who qualifies as an alien enemy, sometimes relying on speculation or misinformation to make that determination. 

Others said they feared their children would be denied citizenship because a member of the parents' extended family was connected to a gang in their home country, even though the parents were not gang members. 

Uncertainty surrounding the order left them with confusion and fear, the families said. 

They were joined in the lawsuit by We Are CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project and the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection. 

The administration's attorneys argued that the request to block the order was premature and said the federal agencies tasked with enforcing it would use “appropriate measures” to do so, relying on official guidance that hasn't been issued yet. 

The judge rejected that argument. 

“No matter what the guidance says, the 2026 Executive Order commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children,” Boardman wrote. 

“The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president’s anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution,” Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a prepared statement. 

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 

___ Associated Press reporter Valerie Gonzalez contributed.
news.summary: A federal judge has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to prohibit automatic U.S. citizenship at birth
news.author: Rebecca Boone

news.title: Volatile electorate delivers mixed results for all parties in latest polls
news.text:
In the two latest new federal polls, Morgan was good for Labor but Essential was bad. There were four federal polls taken last week, largely before the Western Australian Secret Harbour byelection.

The total vote for One Nation and the Coalition was 44% in Morgan (down four), 49% in Newspoll (up two), 49% in Essential (up two) and 50% in Redbridge (down three). The previous Redbridge was probably an outlier, so currently only Morgan doesn’t suggest the right is trending higher.

A NSW DemosAU state poll still has Labor in a dominant position, due to the split right vote and NSW’s optional preferential system.

In Canada, the centre-left governing Liberals easily won all three of Monday’s byelections (two holds and one gain from the Conservatives). US president Donald Trump has helped the Canadian Liberals remain dominant.

Essential poll

A national Essential poll, conducted August 26–30 from a sample of 1,017, gave Labor 26% of the primary vote (down five since the late July Essential poll), the Coalition 26% (up four), One Nation 23% (down two), the Greens 13% (up one), all Others 6% (steady) and undecided 5% (up one).

By respondent preferences, the Coalition led Labor by 50–45, reversing a 48–47 Labor lead in July. This is the Coalition’s biggest lead in an Essential poll since March 2024, and their biggest lead from any pollster this term.

Applying 2025 election preference flows to the primaries would put the Coalition just ahead by about 50.5–49.5. Weak respondent flows to Labor and a low Others vote are features of Essential’s polls.

Anthony Albanese’s net approval slumped seven points to -21 (56% disapprove, 35% approve). This is a record low for him in this poll. Angus Taylor’s improved three points to -9 (41% disapprove, 32% approve).

Just 9% said they were union members and 4% political party members, while 15% were members of local sporting clubs and 11% other voluntary organisations. But 60% said unions were important for working people today (down four since July 2024).

By 55–6, respondents thought violence against women in Australia has increased rather than decreased in the last few years.

Morgan poll

A national Morgan poll, conducted August 24–30 from a sample of 1,585, gave Labor 29.5% of the primary vote (up 2.5 since the August 17–23 Morgan poll), One Nation 23.5% (down 3.5), the Coalition 20.5% (down 0.5), the Greens 13.5% (down 0.5) and all Others 13% (up two).

By respondent preferences, Labor led One Nation by 55.5–44.5, a 2.5-point gain for Labor. Labor led the Coalition by 56–44, a four-point gain for Labor. By 2025 election preference flows, Labor led the Coalition by 55–45, a 2.5-point gain for Labor.

Additional questions from Redbridge poll

I previously covered the late August national Redbridge poll for The Financial Review. In additional questions, Albanese’s net favourability was up two points since late July to -17 (48–31 unfavourable), Pauline Hanson’s was down two points to -12 (48–36 unfavourable) and Taylor’s was up three points to -3 (25–22 unfavourable).

Combining the Coalition and One Nation against Labor and the Greens on the issues, the right led on cost of living by 40–33, housing affordability by 38–31, immigration by 54–24, crime by 45–24, the economy by 43–29, tax reform by 39–29 and national security by 44–26.

The left’s two leads were on healthcare by 39–34 and climate change by 44–25. Since late July, the left has gained, recovering the lead on healthcare.

The top three issues were cost of living (75% said it was a top three issue for them), healthcare (37%) and housing affordability (33%). Immigration has moved into fourth place on 27%, replacing crime.

NSW DemosAU poll

The New South Wales state election is in March 2027. A DemosAU and Premier National poll, conducted August 19–26 from a sample of 1,028, gave Labor 33% of the primary vote (steady since the mid-June DemosAU poll), the Coalition 25% (up five), One Nation 23% (down four), the Greens 13% (steady) and all Others 7% (down one).

Labor is advantaged by the split in the right-wing vote under NSW’s optional preferential system. Based on 2023 election flows, Labor leads the Coalition by 57–43 after preferences.

Half of the 42 upper seats are elected at each election by statewide proportional representation with preferences. In this poll, Labor had 31% in the upper house (up one), the Coalition 25% (up five), One Nation 24% (down three), the Greens 14% (up one) and Legalise Cannabis 2% (up one), with no other party above 1%.

On these vote shares, the pollster estimates Labor would win seven of the 21 upper house seats up next March, the Coalition five, One Nation five and the Greens three with one in doubt. Overall, Labor would have 15 seats out of 42, the Coalition 12, One Nation five, the Greens five, others four and one in doubt. Three of the four others are right-wing.

If this occurred, the overall left would have 21 of the 42 upper house seats, one short of a majority. If the left won the in doubt seat, they would have a majority.

Labor Premier Chris Minns’ net positive score was +15 (37% positive, 22% negative). Liberal leader Kellie Sloane’s was +5 (25% positive, 20% negative). Minns led Sloane as preferred premier by 44–26. By 55–27, respondents supported the NSW gun buyback scheme.

Liberals easily win three Canadian federal byelections

Byelections occurred in three Canadian federal seats on Monday. The centre-left Liberals easily won all three, holding two and gaining one from the Conservatives. This gives them a parliamentary majority with 173 of the 343 seats. A further six byelections are expected in the near future.

I covered these byelections for The Poll Bludger, and also wrote about the upcoming US midterm elections and a possible parliamentary majority for the populist right AfD at a German state election this Sunday.
news.summary: Recent polls carry good news and bad news for all parties – and their leaders.

news.title: Donald Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as 'Trump Strait'
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Wednesday (Sep 2) suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as "Trump Strait", asserting US control of the vital waterway even as fighting raged there with Iran.

It is the latest in a series of geographical name changes floated by Trump, and comes after he claimed US sovereignty over the strait that Tehran has effectively shut for six months.

"Now that we have it under USA control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be 'hotter' than ever before!" Trump said on his Truth Social network.

The White House later posted a map of the Gulf on social media with the waterway marked "Trump Strait".

"It's got a nice ring to it," the White House post added.

The 80-year-old president's call to unilaterally rename an international body of water after himself comes despite the fact that the six-month-old war with Iran shows no sign of ending.

Since returning to office last year, Trump has made a string of similar renaming suggestions, which started out as apparent attempts to troll his adversaries, but then came to fruition.

Last week, the 80-year-old Republican signed an order renaming Lake Ontario as "Lake America" amid a trade war with neighbouring Canada.

Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the "Gulf of America" on his first day back in the White House in January 2025. Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes.

Trump additionally reverted the name of Denali, North America's highest peak, to its former moniker Mt McKinley.

FIGHTING HAS FLARED AGAIN

The billionaire president has also gone on a spree of renaming things after himself, including the Kennedy arts centre in Washington, a peace institute, a "Trump Gold Card" for immigration and a "Trump Rx" drug-sales website.

The US Treasury meanwhile on Wednesday issued US$1 coins featuring Trump's face to mark the 250th anniversary of US independence, running counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency.

But the strait suggestion may also be aimed at providing a fresh distraction from the Iran war, which has caused oil prices to spike for US consumers ahead of crucial midterm elections in November.

Fighting has flared again after weeks of calm, with US forces launching fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in response to what Trump said were new minelaying efforts by Iran.

Iran said one of the US strikes killed four people at a wedding, branding it a "war crime", and launched a wave of retaliatory strikes at US bases in Jordan, the UAE, Kuwait, Bahrain and Iraq.

Iran has effectively shut down the chokepoint, through which a fifth of the world's oil passes, in retaliation for the war Trump started along with Israel in late February.

Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a "new US territory".

Source: AFP
news.summary: Donald Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as 'Trump Strait'
news.author: Hazari Editor

news.title: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two Filipino sailors, Saudi Arabia says
news.text:
Saudi Arabia has condemned what it said was an Iranian attack on a Saudi-owned supertanker on Monday night that killed two Filipino sailors.

The Saudi national shipping company, Bahri, confirmed on Wednesday that its vessel Sidr was "involved in a security incident while transiting the Strait of Hormuz".

Sidr was hit by projectiles north of Oman's Musandam Peninsula, according to maritime security firms. A South Korean-owned supertanker, Senegal Prosperity, was reportedly struck east of Musandam around the same time.

Iran has not responded to the Saudi allegation. But it said earlier that two tankers had caught fire after hitting mines while using an unauthorised route through the strait.

The news of the sailors' deaths came after the US military carried out a wave of air strikes on Iran and Iranian forces targeted US bases in neighbouring Arab states with missiles and drones in their biggest exchange of fire since July.

On Wednesday Iran's health minister said 18 people were killed and 108 injured in the US attacks. Iran has accused the US of a "war crime" over a strike that killed four people including two children at a wedding party in the southern city of Sirik. The US military said it was looking into the reports.

Shipping company Bahri's statement said the unspecified "security incident" affecting Sidr happened in the Strait of Hormuz at around 23:40 local time (19:40 GMT) on Monday.

"It is with profound sadness that Bahri confirms the loss of two of its Filipino seafarers as a result of the incident," it added. “The company extends its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathies to their families, loved ones, and colleagues during this difficult time.”

Later, the Saudi foreign ministry expressed the kingdom's condemnation of "Iran's targeting of the Saudi tanker (Sidr) while it was transiting the Strait of Hormuz".

It also condemned the recent Iranian attacks on Jordan, Bahrain and Kuwait, and stressed the "need to halt escalation and respect the security and safety of international navigation", as well as the security of global energy supplies, national sovereignty, and international law.

The statements were issued a day after maritime risk management and intelligence firms Marisks and Kpler reported that two tankers each loaded with two million barrels of Saudi crude oil were struck by unknown projectiles within minutes of each other as they transited outbound through the Strait of Hormuz late on Monday.

Sidr was struck by "unknown projectiles" at 19:52 GMT about 16 nautical miles (30km) north-east of Khasab, Oman, while Senegal Prosperity was struck by "three unknown projectiles" about 17 nautical miles east of Khasab, according to Marisks.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency also reported two incidents in the same locations.

On Wednesday, Iran's Islamic Revolution Guard Corps said in a statement that two oil tankers sought "at the urging of the US military to transit via an illegal route" in the Strait of Hormuz before "striking mines and exploding". The vessels were "currently on fire", it added.

The US military has not commented, but it said the latest strikes on Iran followed "recent attempted attacks by the IRGC against commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and against American service members".

The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, has effectively been closed since the start of the US and Israel's war with Iran in February due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US blockade of Iranian ports.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

Iran has insisted it will not give up some measure of control over the waterway and has targeted vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters.

Despite the Iranian attacks, US President Donald Trump has declared that the strait is "open" and the US military has been helping ships navigate the southern route.

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said 17 million barrels of oil flowed through the Strait of Hormuz by ship on Monday - a record daily total since the start of the war.

Source: BBC
news.summary: Iranian attack on Saudi tanker killed two Filipino sailors, Saudi Arabia says

news.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump Admin Moves To Revoke Tax Exempt Status For Racially Discriminatory Schools
news.text:
The Treasury Department and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) are expected to roll out regulations that would end the federal tax-exempt status for private schools that discriminate on the basis of race rather than rewarding merit, the Daily Caller learned. 

The Treasury and the IRS will issue the proposed regulations Thursday based on President Donald Trump’s executive orders that aim to restore merit and end discriminatory practices, an administration official told the Caller. (RELATED: Here’s How Trump Has Put ‘Radical’ DEI In The ‘Dustbin’ Throughout 2025)

This rule would apply to private schools that participate in racially discriminatory practices across admissions, scholarships, athletics, loans, educational policies, and other school-administered programs. The rule could affect as many as 18,000 private schools, the official told the Caller.

There are several well-documented instances of race-based discrimination in private schooling. The Department of Justice (DOJ) review of internal policies, email correspondence, and other publicly available materials found that the Yale University School of Medicine had discriminated based on race in its admissions process. Similar cases of discrimination were found at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences as well as the Duke University School of Law. 

The IRS and Treasury cited longstanding Supreme Court precedents set in Brown v. Board of Education, Bob Jones University v. United States, and Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard. 

Although these cases established precedent to eliminate tax-exempt status based on an institution’s discriminatory status, the proposal allows private schools to maintain certain curricula and observances based on genuine religious affiliation. 

Schools would still be able to expand educational and assistance programs for students using criteria based on income, geographic location, individual hardship, first-generation status, military status, or academic achievement, so long as it is race-neutral. 

This rule would apply to taxable years beginning May 31, 2027.
news.summary: EXCLUSIVE: Trump Admin To Revoke Tax Exempt Status For Racially Discriminatory Schools
news.author: Rebeka Zeljko

news.title: Trump Crypto Ally David Bailey's Bitcoin Bet Lost 99% Of Its Stock Value. Now He's Rebuilding The Business.
news.text: David Bailey's Nakamoto is shifting away from the financing model that helped turn it into one of the most prominent Bitcoin treasury companies, searching instead for businesses that generate cash after its shares collapsed about 99% from their 2025 peak.Bailey, a crypto entrepreneur who helped build industry support for President Donald Trump, told Bloomberg that Nakamoto is looking for acquisitions that can improve income and cash flow while supporting its broader Bitcoin strategy. With the stock now trading below the value of the company's Bitcoin holdings, issuing new shares to finance additional cryptocurrency purchases has become far less attractive.The company was created through the merger of Bailey's Nakamoto Holdings with healthcare company KindlyMD, a transaction initially backed by a $510 million private investment and $200 million in convertible notes.Nakamoto's finances deteriorated sharply as Bitcoin prices fell and investor enthusiasm for digital-asset treasury companies faded. news.title: Trump Signs Stopgap Bill to Fund Government Through Midterms
news.text:
President Donald Trump on Sept. 2 signed legislation to fund the government until the midterm elections wrap up in November.

Trump’s Rapid Response team announced that the legislation had been signed in a post on X.

“On Wednesday, September 2, 2026, the President signed into law the ‘Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2027,’ which includes a short-term continuing resolution that provides fiscal year 2027 appropriations to Federal agencies through December 11, 2026, for continuing projects and activities of the Federal Government, and extends authorities for a broad range of programs including surface transportation and veteran programs.”

Often, stopgap funding bills pass relatively painlessly through Congress on election years in the immediate lead-up to the midterms, as lawmakers seek to avoid government shutdowns just before an election.

The legislation sets guardrails for the Department of War, prohibiting it from initiating new programs, increasing production rates, or entering into multi-year procurement.

It permits spending above the default rate, where necessary, to maintain certain programs, including the Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children.

The bill prohibits the Office of Management and Budget from issuing or finalizing its proposed Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance. It stated that if the rule is finalized before the measure’s enactment, it “shall not have force or take effect” through Dec. 11. The rule was published in the Federal Register on May 29.

Other provisions include delaying a ban on hemp for a month. While the Trump administration pushed for the delay, conservatives in Congress oppose it.

House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) has defended the continuing resolution.

“We’re going to avoid the threat of another Democrat shutdown,” he said at a press conference on Sept. 1.

Johnson said the continuing resolution is to give appropriators more time to hash out a full-year budget bill.

“Republicans have made remarkable progress towards returning to regular order and restoring the appropriations process the way it’s supposed to work—to a committee-driven approach, as it should be,” he said.

“And our appropriators have worked very hard to restore that muscle memory, and we are really, really grateful for their work because that is how you act as a good steward of taxpayer dollars and resources, and we’re going to continue all that great work.”

Ahead of the vote, Democrats also expressed support for the continuing resolution.

House Democratic Conference Chairman Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) said there would be bipartisan support for the measure, and Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) urged her fellow Democrats during a caucus meeting to vote in favor of the measure.
news.summary: It would fund the government through Dec. 11.

news.title: Chevron, Eni commit to expand oil projects in Venezuela under US eye
news.text:
CARACAS: US’ Chevron, Italy’s Eni and other foreign energy producers committed on Wednesday to major project expansions to boost oil output in Venezuela, in a signing ceremony in Caracas overseen by interim President Delcy Rodriguez and US Energy Secretary Chris Wright.

The deals are separate from a controversial Caracas-Washington deal recently unveiled that gives the US access to 17 oilfields. Most of the pacts announced on Wednesday relate to project expansions that have been in negotiation with Venezuela’s oil ministry and state oil company PDVSA as part of the migration of dozens of energy contracts to new terms under a sweeping oil reform approved in January.

Still, the signings represents the latest effort by private companies with a longstanding presence in Venezuela to help the country revive its struggling oil industry, which currently produces about 1.25 million barrels per day, far short of its 3 million bpd peak reached in the late 1990s.

READ MORE: Trump to meet US oil execs as Iran war keeps price high

Most oil majors have eschewed major investment in the country for years, retreating after a 2007 nationalization. The industry has also faltered due to lack of investment, mismanagement and sanctions imposed by the US, which is now spearheading a $100 billion investment plan that officials claim will double Venezuela’s output in coming years.

“We are trying to work at what I call Trump-speed. President (Donald) Trump didn’t want a nudge or a slow drift in a positive direction. He wanted to see as fast as possible transformation in Venezuela,” Wright said.

Chevron CEO Mike Wirth and Eni CEO Claudio Descalzi also traveled to Venezuela for the signing. It was Wirth’s first visit to the South American country, where Chevron has maintained a consistent presence in Venezuela even after other oil majors left following the seizure of assets under former President Hugo Chavez.

Chevron plans to invest more than $7 billion to double its output in the country to about 600,000 bpd over the next five years, part of its strategy of expanding joint ventures with PDVSA.

In addition, GE Vernova signed a power sector alliance, which Rodriguez singled out due to the country’s struggles with a large electricity deficit that has left households without electricity for hours and hobbled key industries.

Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt was not seen at the ceremony, days after his company NABEP signed the separate deal with Washington to gain access to a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

Bulky investments

Eni, which shares an offshore gas project with Repsol and a shallow water oil project with PDVSA, will expand to the large Junin 5 heavy oil area in the Orinoco Belt, where it plans to invest $1.5 billion, industry sources said.

As part of its deal, Eni’s current joint venture with PDVSA will transition into a 25-year production sharing contract, the company said in a release.

“What we need is not just signing papers, we need barrels,” Descalzi said during the event.

Junin 5 currently produces approximately 12,000 bpd, Eni said in the release. Oil production target from all its oil projects is 400,000 bpd by the end of this decade.

Other pacts include an oilfield development agreement with energy firm Primavera and an exploration agreement with Denver-based oil services company Aspect Holdings.

news.title: US pounds Iran, Tehran strikes back at bases
news.text:
WASHINGTON/DUBAI: Iranians and their Arab neighbours feared a return of war on Wednesday after the biggest exchange of fire between Tehran and Washington since July, with US forces striking Iran’s southern coast and Iran firing at American bases across the region.

The United States threatened more devastating strikes. Iran accused Washington of hitting a wedding party, killing four people and wounding dozens. Its health minister later said 18 people in total had been killed and 108 injured in the latest wave of US strikes.

Asian and European stocks tumbled after the airstrikes, though Wall Street opened higher as investors focused instead on AI developments.

READ MORE: US military says it completed latest wave of strikes on Iran

Oil prices were marginally firmer in a volatile session that had earlier seen them hit levels not reached since July, amid concerns over the impact of the war on the global economy.

‘Like the end of the world’

The US military said it struck air defences, radar systems, maritime assets, mine-laying capabilities and communications sites on Tuesday. Iran reported hits on multiple targets near the Strait of Hormuz.

“Last night was like the end of the world,” Mahmoud, 38, a municipal worker in Sirik County along the strait, told Reuters by telephone, describing attacks on the area that includes the city where the wedding was reported to have been hit.

Iran responded by striking what it said were US assets in Bahrain, Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq, and said its aim was now to drive US forces from the vast network of military bases they have occupied for decades across the Middle East.

“American evil in the region will be met with heavier, more widespread, and devastating responses, and any country that cooperates with the aggressive American army must accept its dangerous consequences,” Iran’s military command said.

Iran said it killed US forces in Jordan and at a base in northern Iraq, but US officials told Reuters there had not been any casualties, according to initial assessments.

In Kuwait, Iran said it had carried out a missile and drone attack on the vast US Ali Al Salem Air Base and targeted the accommodation of a US commander. Kuwait’s fire service said it put out a blaze at a residential complex hit by a drone.

Qatar, home of the largest US airbase in the Gulf, said it held Iran responsible for attacks and their repercussions. Bahrain, which houses the regional headquarters of the US Navy, said Iranian drones were intercepted and destroyed.

Iran also said two tankers had been struck by mines while being steered through the Strait of Hormuz by US personnel.

Washington says that despite Iranian attacks it is guiding ships through the strait: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said more than 17 million barrels of oil exited on Monday.

Iran blacklisted 11 more ships, bringing the total number of such vessels to 56, a government website showed, meaning it would consider them subject to fines, confiscation or detention if they try to sail through the Strait of Hormuz without Tehran’s permission.

However, US President Donald Trump repeated his assertion that the strait, which handled 20 percent of global oil and liquefied gas shipments before the war, was open to shipping.

“Now that we have it under USA. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT???,” Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Iran says wedding struck

Iranians were fearful that the new strikes signalled war could restart at full throttle.

“It’s very difficult to live like this. We don’t know when America will strike,” Mahpari, 28, a woman in the southern port city of Bandar Abbas, told Reuters by phone.

Iran said four people including a 4-year-old were killed while celebrating a wedding at a home in Sirik. Iranian media said as many as 68 people were wounded there, and released images of injured children in hospital.

Reuters was unable to independently verify the incident.

US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a spokesperson for Central Command, said: “We are aware of reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The US military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” referring to Iran’s Revolutionary Guards.

Video filmed by Iran’s West Asia News Agency at the purported site showed rubble strewn across rooms and a courtyard. A pair of strappy women’s dress sandals lay abandoned on a blood-soaked carpet.

“I am just glad the casualties weren’t even worse,” said Ali Molahi, identified as the father of the bride.

Conflict draining both sides

The exchange of fire was the worst since July, when Trump abruptly halted two weeks of intense bombing of Iran after warnings from his military brass that they were using up munitions and running out of meaningful targets.

Trump has yet to achieve the aims he set when launching “Operation Epic Fury” in February — to end Iran’s nuclear programme, deprive it of the ability to strike its neighbours and create conditions for Iranians to topple their rulers.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Washington was looking at targeting airlines, the maritime industry and digital assets as part of a campaign to increase economic pressure on Tehran.

Iran’s currency has dropped to a record low of more than 2.2 million rials per US dollar, two websites tracking the free market showed on Wednesday. It has lost about 10 percent in the past week alone.

Sources have told Reuters Trump aides are trying to keep the war quiet for now to avert a rout in congressional elections in November. Polls show Americans oppose the war by more than a two-to-one margin.

news.title: Trump floats renaming Strait of Hormuz as ‘Trump Strait’
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday suggested renaming the Strait of Hormuz as “Trump Strait” despite the fact that the crucial waterway remains contested amid the war with Iran.

“Now that we have it under U.S.A. control, should we change the name Hormuz Strait to TRUMP STRAIT??? Like America itself, it would be ‘hotter’ than ever before!” Trump said on his Truth Social network.

It is the latest geographical name change floated by Trump and comes a week after he ordered Lake Ontario to be renamed as “Lake America” amid a trade war with Canada.

READ ALSO: Trump says US gave Iran many chances, dismisses value of any deal, reports Fox News

Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” on his first day back in office in January 2025.

Neither Mexico nor Canada have accepted the changes.

Many of the previous name changes started off as apparently jovial remarks by the 80-year-old US president before he then followed through to make them a reality.

Trump has in recent weeks repeatedly pressed a threat to claim sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, even posting a map showing the waterway as a “new US territory.”

But Iran has effectively shut down the chokepoint, through which a fifth of the world’s oil passes, in retaliation for the war Trump started along with Israel in late February.

Oil prices are rising again after US forces launched fresh strikes near the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday in response to what Trump said were new minelaying efforts by Iran.

news.title: US postal whistleblower warns ballot system could disrupt midterms
news.text:
WASHINGTON: A US Postal Service whistleblower has warned that millions of Americans could be prevented from receiving mail ballots ahead of November’s midterm elections because of a rushed, new system ordered by President Donald Trump and due for launch Tuesday.

The anonymous federal official alleges that the agency has continued developing the system despite court orders blocking key parts of Trump’s effort to impose new federal controls on voting by mail.

The disclosure, released Tuesday by Democratic US Senator Richard Blumenthal, describes the project as “secretive, rushed, chaotic, and fundamentally flawed” and warns that insufficient testing could lead to “catastrophic failure.”

news.title: US Treasury issues USD1 coin with Trump’s face on it
news.text:
WASHINGTON: The US Treasury on Wednesday issued USD 1 coins featuring the face of President Donald Trump, the latest move in an unprecedented campaign by the Republican billionaire to put his personal stamp on national institutions.

The coins were minted to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States celebrated this year.

A roll of 25 USD 1 coins was available for sale for USD 61 — a mark-up of 144 percent — with a 100-coin bag available for USD 154.50.

When the Treasury announced the plan it was unclear if the coins would have monetary value or would be purely commemorative, but on Wednesday the US Mint said the coins were “also in circulation.”

The move to put Trump’s countenance on a coin with monetary value runs counter to federal law that says no living president may appear on US currency.

Trump has aggressively defied precedent and legal challenges in his push to remake US institutions in his second term, putting his name on the Kennedy Center for the Arts and demolishing the East Wing of the White House to make room for a new ballroom, among other moves.

The new coin features Trump’s face on one side, with the words “Liberty” and “In God We Trust.” It also features the dates 1776-2026, marking 250 years of US independence.

news.title: Thought leadership: real or self-styled?
news.text:
After every few years management gurus, scientists and practitioners come up with some “new” fancy jargon, cliché or a coinage. This I believe is done to remain relevant and meaningful to the dynamics of change happening in every sphere of life. Upon closer examination it is either old wine in new bottle or a cocktail of over-lapping concepts that tastes the same but appears new and appealing.

Over the last decade or so, we have seen how the concept of leadership has been broken down into several layers of recognition. A ‘simple leader’ of the past, with all the related skills and virtues attending that persona, is now required to seek recognition through the hair-splitting of leadership concepts. Consequently, we have situational, transformational, servant, parental, and humble leadership. What beats all these fine distinctions, however, is the leadership termed ‘authentic.’ What?

There can be unauthentic persons but how can anyone be a non-authentic leader? This one feature must disrobe him/her of any leadership position held. This is in my view managerial blasphemy, proving bankruptcy of managerial ability to develop sound alternative concept or thought.

Leadership, conceptually, is not medical science, where more and more of less and less leads to ‘specialisation’. While a doctor may start as a general surgeon, they require specialized education and clinical experience to qualify as a specialist, such as a cardiac surgeon, an ENT surgeon, a liver surgeon, or a nephrologist. Leadership, on the contrary, is a wholesome concept; being IT specialist does not lend the person to be addressed as a ‘leader’. Leadership requires more than specialisation.

Much before this division and hair splitting, there are some primary requirements which must be met to be called a ‘leader’. All leaders need to have certain basic qualities in their personality like abilities to draw a vision, strategies and have sound communication skills, a minimum standard of technical proficiency of the relevant industry and be possessed of ability to collect the right people (human resources) and organise them towards the achievement of the goals and objectives and, above all, have in possession and display a very deep sense of integrity and honesty. Besides these minimum, there are several other characteristics and ingredients that go towards the making of a leader.

Hence adding any prefix to the word ‘leader’ is to confirm, firstly, the presence of all qualities required to be called a leader. A thought leader, hence, is a concept like other branches of leadership traits, where it pre-supposes that the basic criteria of leadership standards stand ticked.

As an example, if in the economy there are say 25 pharmaceutical companies operating, each of them would have a CEO/MD, who by sheer positional power are ‘leaders’ in their own right. But not all of them can be classified as ‘thought leaders’.

As a society, mostly we are generous and hence have this propensity streak of bestowing unbelievable titles and accolades upon people. Doing the necessary is no outstanding performance. This is done with wanton indiscrimination. Those who may not have performed or may have done the bare minimum necessarily required to be done are recognised with civil awards.

So who is a thought leader?

Many thoughtless individuals who never ventured into the difficult task of ‘thinking’ are introduced as ‘thought leaders’. For readers easy discernment of this predicament of who qualifies as a thought leader. Compare US Presidents Donald Trump and JFK. The former thinks after the event; the latter was a genuine thought leader.

A thought leader is someone who is widely recognised as an authority or a specialist (expert) who provides to society at large deep insights coupled with forward-looking ideas that serve as a bait of inspiration to influence others in a specific field or industry. Such individuals are possessed of abilities to thinking in their area of interest with a view to creating a body of knowledge or thoughts based upon experience and practice.

Thought leaders in specific industries/fields offer solutions that are new to issues of cobweb complexities. They are usually respected and well regarded for their analyses and judgments. And, possibly and more importantly, thought leaders are essentially great communicators; they are clear headed, hence possess the quality to articulate their thoughts with clarity and conciseness.

Having ‘thought’ on issues that could be of value is one thing but to be able to wire them across the industry is different. The thought leader is someone who is willing to state and defend his/her opinion.

Thought leaders walk their talk. Noble thoughts cannot be backed by ignoble behaviour. They must remain strong adherents to their thoughts. Consistency is their virtue. This is a pre-requisite. In the political arena, I find only Jinnah and Z.A. Bhutto as thought leaders and to a lesser degree, Benazir Bhutto. Thought leaders ought to be genuine, truthful, authentic and empowering. The detractors of Z.A. Bhutto may find him a little short on some of these traits, but even history cannot deny him the credit for having aroused the political consciousness of the masses, just as our founder did in rallying the Muslims of India toward a common objective. Both sold well their narratives.

Thought leaders are attentive listeners. While they can eloquently express, they are mostly active lender of their ears. Their skill lies in being able to sift through the mine(s) of data and arrive at workable/doable solutions. They do not impose but exhibit enormous patience with their audience to gain their confidence.

Thought leaders’ focus of attention zeros in on a defined parameter, which usually is short and not too widened area. This allows them attention of the specific audience. A thought leader from the aviation industry would have none or limited appeal to those outside the sphere of avionics; however, an HR thought leader may have larger audiences that cuts across industries and disciplines. Human resource peculiarities are normally common amongst many different set of enterprises.

In any organisation, there are ‘thought leaders who could be recognisable on the ladder of corporate hierarchy or they could be obscure to the management but not to co-workers. We find many individuals who are on de facto basis real thought leaders, to whom colleagues are willing to go to seek and learn. Thought leaders develop for themselves over a period of time their credibility through public appearances or by way of posting credible content on various social media sites; many do so by running vlogs or their own channels. Thought leaders are invited to seminars and conferences, which gives them both the trust of their followers and greater visibility. Popular thought leaders today include Bill Gates in the IT and communications industry, Mark Zuckerberg in the social media sphere, and Simon Sinek in the field of inspirational leadership, who authored the bestselling book Start With Why. Historically, Confucius is recognized for promoting moral standards, family duty, and harmony; Karl Marx for his critical theories against capitalism; and Martin Luther King Jr. for his peaceful activism for racial equality. I have deliberately avoided thought leaders from the arena of religion, where there are many outstanding ones.

In conclusion, it needs to be reiterated that every single thought leader must necessarily possess all the traits, characteristics, skills and abilities that a Leader, must have to firstly qualify as a ‘leader’, and thence only he/she can graduate to being a ‘thought leader’. To call or refer to someone as ‘thought leader’ mustn’t be an act of charity or self-deception; it must meet the litmus test of having in the persona the basics of leadership.

(The writer is a Senior Banker & Freelance Columnist)

news.title: Donald Trump Beats Zohran Mamdani on Net Favorability: New Poll
news.text: President Donald Trump has a more favorable net favorability rating than New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, according to a new Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, though both men are underwater among voters as two of the most recognizable faces of their respective parties. Trump has a net favorability rating of -8 percent, with 42 percent of registered voters viewing him favorably and 50 percent unfavorably, according to the poll. Mamdani, meanwhile, has a net favorability rating of -14 percent, with 25 percent viewing him favorably and 39 percent unfavorably. The poll surveyed 2,100 registered voters from August 28-30, 2026, and has a margin of error of 2.1 percent. The numbers are notable because Trump and Mamdani have become defining figures for the Republican and Democratic parties, respectively. Trump has reshaped the GOP around his Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, while Mamdani's rapid rise has made him one of the most prominent figures associated with the Democratic Party's progressive wing. Newsweek reached out to the White House and Mamdani's office via email on Wednesday for comment. What To Know The Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll found that 51 percent of voters believe the Democratic Party is being taken over by the far left, while 45 percent believe the Republican Party is being taken over by the far right. Mamdani's rise has nevertheless represented a significant shift within the Democratic Party. His progressive agenda and upset victory over establishment Democrat Andrew Cuomo in New York's mayoral primary have made him a national political figure, while also fueling debate over whether Democrats should embrace his brand of politics or distance themselves from it. Trump faces a similar dynamic on the Republican side, where his continued dominance has made it somewhat difficult for the party to separate itself from his agenda and political style. The result is a striking political paradox: Trump and Mamdani may be among the clearest faces of America's increasingly polarized parties, but neither is viewed favorably by a majority of Americans, according to the new poll. As both parties look toward the 2026 midterm elections, the question may be whether voters want more of the political movements these two men represent—or something different altogether. Grant Davis Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek via email on Wednesday, "This probably reflects the fact that President Trump and the Republicans have made socialism and Mamdani a central target of their negative messaging in recent weeks. It’s having an effect, apparently." "Mamdani is also actually making changes, and has had some glitches with staff, etc., and as those mount that will take some shine off of the 'young phenom' effect he’s been enjoying. But that doesn’t explain the national numbers, because most Americans don’t follow day-to-day policy and politics in NYC," he added. When asked if Americans view both Trump and Mamdani as leaders of their party, Reeher later said, "The president is always the de facto leader of his party. Trump is no different, but there are divisions within the ranks, on both the Iran war and the tariffs. I don’t see Mamdani as the recognized 'leader' of the Democratic Party, and doubt he ever will be. He’s one of the principal leaders of the Left wing of the party, that’s for sure. I don’t think the party has a particular leader at the moment, to be honest." Florida Atlantic University politics professor Craig Agranoff also told Newsweek on Wednesday when asked about the net favorability numbers, "A month-to-month flip like this is not shocking." "National favorability for both men moves with the news cycle, and Mamdani is still building name recognition outside New York. Trump remains far better known, so his numbers are more settled even when they sit underwater. That does not make either man the uncontested leader of his party. Trump is still the central figure on the Republican side because he occupies the White House and defines the coalition," Agranoff added. "Mamdani is a rising face of the Democratic left, but the party still has multiple power centers and he does not yet speak for the whole national brand. Favorability gaps this size tell you more about visibility and polarization than about who actually runs either party." Meanwhile, the Harvard CAPS/Harris Poll shows only two U.S. political figures with positive net favorability: Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump's net favorability in the poll is worse than former Vice President Kamala Harris, Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and House Speaker Mike Johnson. The poll shows Trump's net favorability is better than California Governor Gavin Newsom, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, Tucker Carlson and Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan. What Polls Show Other polling, however, has shown that Mamdani's favorability has been positive as he has settled into office. An early-August Siena College poll found 47 percent of New York likely voters viewed him favorably, compared with 44 percent who viewed him unfavorably, while other polling around his first 100 days in office showed 48 percent of New Yorkers approving of his performance and 30 percent disapproving. July's Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed Trump's net favorability at -13 percent, with 40 percent net favorability compared to 53 percent net unfavorability. The poll showed Mamdani with a net favorability of -7 percent, with 27 percent net favorability and 35 percent net unfavorability. That poll surveyed 1,776 registered voters from July 11-12, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.3 percent. A Siena University poll taken in June showed Trump's favorability at 32 percent, compared with 63 percent unfavorable. The survey showed that Mamdani's favorability was positive, at 45 percent, compared to 34 percent unfavorable. The poll surveyed 1,120 New York State registered voters from June 17-23, 2026, and had a margin of error of 3.6 percent. A May Harvard CAPS/Harris poll showed that Trump's net favorability was -6 percent, with a 43 percent net favorable rating compared to 50 percent net unfavorability. Mamdani's net favorability rating was 23 percent compared to a net 33 percent unfavorable rating. Mamdani's overall net favorability in the poll was -10 percent. The poll surveyed 1,725 registered voters from May 29-31, 2026, and had a margin of error of 2.4 percent. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Trump has reshaped the GOP around MAGA, while Mamdani has emerged as a leading figure of the Democratic Party's progressive wing.

news.title: Trump meets with travel industry CEOs on push to boost foreign tourism
news.text: WASHINGTON - U.S. President Donald Trump met with major travel company executives on Wednesday including representatives from American Airlines, Marriott, MGM Resorts and Carnival to discuss ways to reverse a decline in international visitors.U.S. tourism got a big but temporary boost from the FIFA World Cup this summer. news.title: Inside the Plan to Pass a Federal Film Tax Incentive Now That Trump Is Onboard
news.text:
After the latest meeting between an Oscar winner and the President of the United States, the American film industry may finally have a path towards something that has been at the top of its political wish list for years: a federal production tax incentive.

That breakthrough moment might have come on Monday, when President Donald Trump threw his weight behind the idea after speaking with one of his few outspoken Hollywood supporters, actor Jon Voight. After previous meetings between the president and the star of “Coming Home” about the country’s production exodus, Trump floated the idea of imposing tariffs on films produced outside of the U.S.

Now, with Voight’s urging, the president said on Truth Social that he is in favor of the incentive that a handful of lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have been quietly gathering support for over the past 18 months, and Congressional insiders told TheWrap that after next week’s recess, the incentive will be formally introduced as legislation with the hopes of getting it to Trump’s desk by the end of the year.

According to the insiders with knowledge of talks between the White House and House Republicans, the current plan is to introduce the incentive as a bill in the House Ways and Means Committee the week of Sept. 14. The details of the bill will be ironed out between now and then, but the current baseline for the incentive is a 20% tax credit on labor costs for all productions shot in the United States.

Such a program would be a huge salve to an entertainment industry that has watched for decades as competing incentives from overseas has steadily drained the production opportunities in Hollywood and the U.S. While individual states have tried to compete with their own incentives, including a richer program in California, a federal program would encourage more productions to return stateside.

“President Trump has made clear his intention to protect the dominance of the American film industry,” White House spokesperson Kush Desai told TheWrap. “President Trump is committed to Make Hollywood Great Again, and his administration continues to explore all possible policy options to ensure Hollywood remains a potent force of American culture.”

Republicans get the green light

It has been 29 years since Canada established a nationwide tax incentive to coax Hollywood studios to film movies and TV shows like “The X-Files” outside of the United States, and in the decades that followed, especially after the U.K. established its own incentive program in 2007, an increasing number of Hollywood’s most watched titles have been shot in other countries as studios have taken advantage of foreign tax packages that the U.S., with its patchwork of local and state incentives, cannot match. 

Whether because of a lack of political will or the perception that a nationwide credit would primarily benefit an industry associated with liberalism, passing this incentive seemed for years like a long shot. But over the past few days, public bipartisan enthusiasm emerged to push a policy over the finish line that would mark the U.S.’s biggest play in the global competition for film and TV jobs.

The Trump Administration is leaving it to the House GOP to work out the specifics, and among the Republicans on the Ways & Means Committee expected to be involved are Texas’ Nathaniel Moran, New York’s Nicole Malliotakis and Ohio’s Mike Carey.

Given the recent industry developments in those House members’ backyards, that is little surprise. Last year, New York increased the annual cap on its tax credit incentive program to $800 million while Texas increased the state budget allocations for its grant incentive program to $300 million every two years through 2035. In Ohio, which offers a 30% tax credit on eligible spending, Cincinnati was chosen to play Metropolis in James Gunn’s “Superman” and its upcoming sequel, “Man of Tomorrow.”

Outside of Ways & Means, the freshman bipartisan duo expected to run point on the incentive are Georgia Republican Brian Jack and California Democrat Laura Friedman, both of whom come from districts that have suffered from production flight in recent years.

Friedman, a former film producer, represents Burbank, the cradle of Hollywood filmmaking and where much of the tidal wave of grassroots and union organizing from production workers desperate for work has come since the 2023 strikes.

Jack’s district is situated just outside of Atlanta, once one of the most robust production hubs in America with Georgia’s uncapped tax credit program. But production spending in the Peach State has fallen to a 10-year-low as companies like Marvel Studios, which moved production of its “Avengers” movies to England, have pulled up stakes to take advantage of incentive packages in countries that offer tax credits on the federal level.

“My Congressional District is home to Trilith Studios, and I proudly represent the craftsmen, electricians, and carpenters who work hard to create movies that inspire generations of Americans. I applaud President Trump’s leadership in calling for a legislative solution to bring film production back to the United States, and I look forward to working with him and my colleagues in Congress to achieve this important goal,” Jack said in a statement. 

“This is an incentive that will benefit an industry that employes 2.5 million Americans, not to mention supports millions more in businesses that support film and TV productions,” Friedman told TheWrap. “I have had talks with Republicans on [the Ways & Means Committee] and many of them are in filming states, so they understand the importance of this incentive on a nationwide level.” 

Meanwhile, in California…

On the Democratic side, sources said internal talks are still being held on who from the party will join Friedman in leading the charge on the incentive. But it is likely that the Dems’ large California contingent will play a role. Sen. Adam Schiff previously drafted legislation on a federal incentive, and House Dem Chair Jimmy Aguilar and Vice Chair Ted Lieu both expressed their support for the incentive in a press pool on Monday.

Another Democrat to watch is San Gabriel Valley Rep. Judy Chu, who is also on the Ways & Means Committee. In addition to supporting the federal incentive, Chu last year introduced the CREATE Act, a bill she co-authored with Rep. Malliotakis that would renew and strengthen Section 181, a tax law first enacted in 2004 that allowed film and TV producers to deduct up to $15 million in certain production spending. 

The CREATE Act was introduced to the Ways & Means Committee in August 2025, but it hasn’t been picked up since. Consequently, Section 181, the only federal production tax credit on the books, expired at the end of last year. 

“While H.R. 1 extended bonus depreciation to include film and TV productions, that deduction cannot be taken until a production is released. The CREATE Act would allow eligible production costs to be deducted in the year they are paid or incurred, giving producers, particularly independent producers, access to the incentive when they are actually making the investments and creating jobs here in the United States,” Chu said in a statement to TheWrap.

“This is an area where Democrats and Republicans can work together. Congress should act quickly to pass the CREATE Act and establish a new tax credit for American film and television production,” Chu continued.

Once the incentive bill is introduced, it will be pored over by the MPA and lobbyists from other Hollywood entities like the Directors Guild of America and IATSE, among others, who will likely provide further input. Sources said that the MPA has been developing a months-long report on the economic impact of a federal tax incentive that is tentatively set for release in mid-September, around the time that the bill will be introduced.

If and when the bill gets lobbyist approval, expect a full court press from Hollywood, including a potential appearance from DGA President Christopher Nolan, who has been back in the public spotlight all summer with his mammoth box office hit “The Odyssey.”

This may also be the time when the DGA invokes a side letter it negotiated with the Hollywood studios during its labor contract negotiations this summer, with the studios pledging in writing to send some of their top executives to lobby for the federal incentive when deemed appropriate. The studios and their labor reps, the AMPTP, were mum on who exactly from the C-suites would go to Capitol Hill in that scenario, but it is a sign of the all-hands-on-deck approach Hollywood will take once a vote on this industry-changing bill is in reach.

On the political side, though, it is extremely unlikely that the incentive would be passed before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, where prognosticators expect Democrats to take control of the House with control of the Senate currently considered a toss-up. Given the number of committee votes and likely amendments the incentive will go through in both branches of Congress, insiders told TheWrap that mid-November is probably the earliest that the incentive could pass and be ready for Trump to sign into law.

Still, that would be ahead of schedule based on conversations TheWrap has had with several producers and studio execs this year, who had a general sense of optimism that the political will was finally building for a federal incentive, but did not expect serious progress until 2027. That’s why many of the industry statements in response to Trump’s announcement on Monday heaped praise on Voight for using his access to the president to get the ball rolling.

“Jon Voight has also been a strong advocate for bringing more film and television production back to the United States, and we recognize his efforts to advance this important goal,” SAG-AFTRA said in a statement on Tuesday. “We’re encouraged to see the administration recognize the importance of strengthening our domestic production industry and move in this direction.”
news.summary:
Washington insiders say legislation will be introduced in the House of Representatives later this month after a weeklong recess

news.title: Trump Says China ‘Relatively Inactive’ on Iran as Xi, Pezeshkian Hold Brief Talks
news.text:
President Donald Trump said China had been “relatively inactive” during the conflict with Iran, including over the Strait of Hormuz, one day before Chinese leader Xi Jinping held brief talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at a regional summit.

Trump made the remarks at the White House on Aug. 31 while discussing Xi’s expected visit to Washington later this month.

“He’s coming in a couple of weeks. He looks forward to it; I look forward to having him,” Trump said.

“Even with the Strait of Hormuz, he’s relatively inactive. He’s been relatively inactive by comparison to what he could have been,” Trump added.

Asked by The Epoch Times what Chinese actions or restraint Trump was referring to and whether the administration had received any commitments or assurances from Beijing regarding Iran or the Strait of Hormuz, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly referred to Trump’s comments and provided no additional details.

On Sept. 1, Pezeshkian and Xi held what Iran’s presidency described as a brief meeting and conversation on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.

Neither Beijing nor Tehran announced a formal bilateral meeting or released a substantive account of talks between the two leaders.

The limited public interaction differed from their meetings at recent major gatherings.

Xi held a formal meeting with Pezeshkian in Beijing during the 2025 SCO summit. The Chinese Foreign Ministry said the two discussed bilateral relations and cooperation in trade, investment, clean energy and connectivity.

Xi said at the time that Beijing placed relations with Iran “high on its diplomatic agenda in the Middle East.”

The Chinese readout also referred to their previous meeting in Kazan, Russia, during the 2024 BRICS summit.

By comparison, Chinese authorities released a detailed account of Xi’s Aug. 31 meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of this week’s SCO summit.

The limited Xi–Pezeshkian interaction came as China joined the other SCO members in approving a declaration backing Iran on several points.

The SCO said its leaders approved 28 documents at the Sept. 1 summit, including the Bishkek Declaration.

The declaration expressed deep concern over developments involving Iran and reiterated the organization’s position condemning military strikes on Iranian territory, saying the attacks caused civilian casualties and economic damage.

It also backed Iran’s sovereignty and territorial integrity and called for the conflict to be resolved through political and diplomatic means.

The SCO in a July foreign ministers’ statement said it condemned military strikes on Iran and favored a political and diplomatic settlement.

The declaration did not announce a collective military commitment to defend Iran. The SCO Secretariat described the organization after the summit as maintaining a “peace-loving, non-bloc character.”

That distinction is consistent with limits Beijing has placed on its security relationship with Tehran.

A March assessment by the congressionally created U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission said Tehran has sought deeper strategic alignment with Beijing, while China has avoided formal defense commitments.

The commission said Beijing was unlikely to take significant action in support of Iran beyond diplomatic backing and dual-use supplies, while seeking to preserve its broader relationships in the Middle East.

It also said China appeared not to participate in the 2026 iteration of a recurring China–Iran–Russia naval exercise despite earlier reports that the drill would be held around the Strait of Hormuz.

China’s limited direct military role has not ended its importance to Iran’s economy.

The same USCC assessment said China buys roughly 90 percent of Iran’s exported oil and estimated that Chinese purchases generated about $31 billion for Tehran in 2025.

Washington has continued targeting Chinese and Hong Kong entities that help Iran move oil, money, and military-related goods.

On Aug. 24, Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast, a broader campaign aimed at cutting off Iran’s financial connections worldwide.

The accompanying sanctions targeted networks operating across China, Hong Kong, and other jurisdictions. Treasury said Hong Kong- and China-linked companies helped transport Iranian oil, move funds through front companies. and support procurement tied to Iran’s military programs.

Earlier in August, Treasury also sanctioned multiple networks that used Hong Kong shell companies to move hundreds of millions of dollars through Iran’s clandestine banking system.

Trump invited Xi to visit Washington during their May summit in Beijing.

The Congressional Research Service also listed a Sept. 24 Washington visit as planned in its Aug. 26 overview of U.S.–China relations.
news.summary: China joined a declaration condemning strikes on Iran as Xi prepares for an expected Sept. 24 White House meeting with Trump.

news.title: How refreshing to see a film that portrays Churchill as the flawed and uncertain man he really was (even if it was made by the French): PETER HITCHENS
news.text:
Are you as sick as I am of modern films portraying Winston Churchill as a faultless smiley hero, chatting merrily to citizens on the London Tube while the Luftwaffe roars overhead, and also winning all his battles?

These babyish screen depictions make it impossible to understand why King George VI didn’t trust Churchill and why much of the Tory Party pretty much loathed him, or why he was chucked out on his ear by British voters in 1945.

Truly great men, you see, are often misfits, awkward, even rude, and not always likeable, let alone popular. The modern syrupy accounts also don’t explain why Churchill was genuinely brilliant, that despite being profoundly right on several key occasions, he was often wrong. Or how he managed to spend so much of his life as an outcast tottering on the brink of bankruptcy, kept going by handouts from dubious men.

Now, in a fine new French film, De Gaulle: Resistance (in cinemas now), the superb English actor Sir Simon Russell Beale gives us a completely new view – a Churchill who is tricky, wavering, humiliated by the Americans and – gasp – sometimes wrong.

He also speaks French, as badly as I do, which is a joy to hear. Our education system has almost given up on teaching us to speak French. Why bother, as almost every French person now speaks embarrassingly good English? So it is getting harder and harder to experience the awful sound of attempts at French by a ‘Rosbif’ (this is the French equivalent of us calling them ‘Frogs’). Likewise, you now seldom see a French lip curling as an Englishman mangles and tortures the graceful, precise language of Moliere and Victor Hugo.

You may be sure that Charles de Gaulle had to struggle to suppress his horror at Churchill’s attempts to speak French every time they met, even as he struggled to drink the fluid which we then called ‘coffee’. He is said to have asked, given a cup of this substance: ‘Is this perhaps the famous English tea?’

The Frogs – this is very much a French film – make Sir Simon wear some very strange things, including a sort of reddish tweed suit, which would surely have got Churchill horsewhipped on the steps of any good London club he tried to enter. But despite these failings, Sir Simon’s Winston is completely captivating and wholly believable.

The deep irony of this very pro-de Gaulle drama is that it is based on a biography of the General by an Englishman, Julian Jackson. French professors have been fuming for years because Jackson’s account of France’s greatest modern leader is so much better than anything written by a Frenchman. What emerges from it is that de Gaulle was at least as great as Churchill, quite possibly greater as he had, to begin with, nothing at all.

De Gaulle had won France one of its few battlefield successes in its futile attempt to halt the invading Nazis. He became a government minister for war before fleeing across the English Channel in June 1940.

The drama shows Britain’s initial cautious and mean treatment of him, awarding de Gaulle a dingy obscure room from which to work and to rally those few Frenchmen and women who still refused to accept their defeat. We have already seen the General briefly in combat, smashing a column of Nazi tanks with astute leadership and unflinching physical courage under fire, characteristics de Gaulle definitely possessed. So we know that he is not just a very tall, rather forbidding man who smokes too much.

The man who plays him, the French-Armenian actor Simon Abkarian, manages to convey de Gaulle’s giant 6ft 5in stature, even though he only just clears 6ft himself. De Gaulle always fretted that he was just too tall for most people to cope with him. Had he not been so magnificent, he would have been ridiculous. He looked like a camel, aloof and possessing secret knowledge, and he was given to silent brooding as well as to furious argument.

The drama shows Churchill at first browbeaten by his unimaginative War Cabinet into abandoning collaboration with de Gaulle right from the start. It will not be the last time he wants to do this, and it would have been very easy for him to have done so. But having made this mistake once, Churchill, seeing what others cannot see in this man he cannot stand, changes his mind. And so de Gaulle is allowed to make a BBC broadcast from London – the first of many rallying the ‘Free French’ throughout the war – on June 18, 1940, the day after his arrival. This marks the beginning of France’s rebirth.

For years afterwards he would make these broadcasts over and over again, and they gave hope to millions. But although the French came to know his voice as if he were a personal friend, almost nobody in France knew what he looked like, so that when he finally strode into Paris on Liberation Day in 1944, his extraordinary appearance was a complete surprise. Back and forth the two men go, Churchill growling and de Gaulle snapping, de Gaulle demanding the impossible and then himself doing the impossible by establishing bases in France’s muddy, decrepit African empire – and so beginning the defeat of the collaborating traitor Marshal Petain.

Perhaps the climax of the Churchill-de Gaulle struggle is a Downing Street meeting at which the General insists that he is in fact the embodiment of France, a claim Churchill bitingly contests. At this point, the French giant seizes an antique chair, smashes it to bits and storms off to his wife and daughter in Hampstead, there to sulk magnificently until events prove him right.

He is France, to all intents and purposes, crazy as this sounds to us in our world of peace and stability. For this is the true heart of the film. Churchill, who embodies Britain much as his rival embodies France, comes to see that this infuriating, almost crazy junior general does in fact know something about power and kingship which almost nobody else knows.

He also possesses a total ruthlessness and a wild gambler’s courage. Once de Gaulle’s utter refusal to accept defeat began to enter the minds of the French people, he was bound to win.

But it goes deeper still. De Gaulle is hated by Franklin Roosevelt, who is portrayed in this film as a cold, harsh and tricky man, who at one stage prefers Vichy collaborators to de Gaulle because they are more pliant.

Roosevelt is shown icily berating Churchill at a White House meeting for not controlling de Gaulle, much as Donald Trump once berated Ukraine’s President Zelensky. Hearing of this, de Gaulle explains that he defies Roosevelt because, if he does not, even when he is weak and alone, France will end up as an American vassal. He warns that Britain faces the same fate if it is not careful.

And lo, France’s nuclear deterrent in 2026 is designed, made and controlled entirely in France. Ours uses American missiles and US designs, and probably could not be launched without US permission. History has consequences, and this piece of celluloid history has much to tell us.
news.summary: Are you as sick as I am of modern films portraying Winston Churchill as a faultless smiley hero, chatting merrily to citizens on the London Tube while the Luftwaffe roars overhead?

news.title: Ambassador to Brazil affirms that Trump seeks to destroy Cuba
news.text:
Cuba’s Ambassador to Brazil, Víctor Cairo, denounced in an interview published on Wednesday that the U.S. government seeks to destroy Cuba, while treating Latin America and the Caribbean as subordinate territories.

During the interview with Grupo Record, the diplomat stated that the Donald Trump administration has adopted cruel measures, reinforcing, like no other, the aggression against Cuba.

“It is a government determined to destroy our country, which considers Latin America and the Caribbean as inferior peoples subordinate to the interests of the United States,” he asserted.

He acknowledged that, despite the current situation, there have been attempts at dialogue between Havana and Washington, although he described these efforts as very difficult due to what he characterized as the U.S. intention to impose “a model of destruction on Cuba.”

The ambassador maintained that the Caribbean nation remains willing to engage in dialogue with the United States, but only under principles of respect and sovereign equality.

“Cuba does not discuss changes to the U.S. political system, nor to its social problems. Likewise, it does not accept any attempt by the United States to change the Cuban political system,” he stated.

According to the diplomat, Havana is willing to discuss issues such as trade, drug trafficking, and organized crime with Washington, but rejects any form of interference in its internal affairs.

These statements come amidst increasing U.S. aggression against Cuba during Trump’s second term.

The U.S. government has maintained and strengthened the economic, commercial, and financial embargo it has imposed on the island for more than 60 years, and since the beginning of this year, it has added an energy blockade that prevents access to fuel.

In the interview, Cairo referred to the impact of the blockade, mentioning accumulated losses of some $2.1 trillion since 1960, with damages exceeding $7.5 billion between March 2024 and February 2025 and $8 billion in the following 12 months.

He also linked the aforementioned energy embargo to problems with fuel supply and electricity generation, as well as difficulties in ensuring the operation of essential services.

“We are dealing with a country that does not allow oil to enter Cuba. This has a brutal cost for the entire economy. And how do you measure the impact of a mother who gives birth and whose child dies because there is no electricity? How do you measure, economically, the impact of infant mortality in Cuba, which rose in less than seven months from 4 to 9.9 per 1,000 live births?” he asked.

Furthermore, the diplomat highlighted Brazil’s solidarity with Cuba and mentioned the recent shipment of 48 tons of powdered milk via two flights by the Brazilian Air Force, in addition to medicines destined for the Cuban population.
